objectives.name: Configure automation for Microsoft Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel
Configure the Microsoft Sentinel SIEM and platform
Ingest data into the Microsoft Sentinel SIEM and platform
Respond to alerts and incidents in Microsoft Defender XDR
Respond to alerts and incidents in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
Investigate Microsoft 365 activities to identify threats
Detect threats by using Microsoft Defender XDR
Detect threats by using the Microsoft Sentinel platform

lessons.title: Defender XDR email notifications
lessons.short: Defender XDR can email people about new **incidents**, about **response actions**, and about new or updated **Threat analytics** reports. All three are rule-based and live under Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Email notifications, each on its own tab.
lessons.deep:
Email notifications let a SOC react without watching the portal all day. In the Microsoft Defender portal go to **Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Email notifications**. There are three tabs:
- **Incidents**: an incident notification rule has Basics (name), Notification settings (alert **severity**, **device group scope**, optional filtering by service/detection source, **Send only one notification per incident**, **Include organization name**, **Include tenant-specific portal link**), Recipients, and Review. Use **Send test email** to check delivery.
- **Actions**: notifies when response actions run. Filter by **action source** (Manual, Automated or both), the actions themselves, device groups, and **action status** (Completed, Failed).
- **Threat analytics**: notify on all new or updated reports, or only reports of a certain type or tag (for example ransomware).

You need the **Manage security settings** permission (Security Administrator or higher under basic permissions). With RBAC you can only create, edit and receive notifications for device groups you are allowed to manage. Recipients only get emails for incidents that occur after they are added.

terms.d: Rule that emails chosen recipients when incidents matching severity, source and device group conditions are created or updated.

terms.t: Send only one notification per incident
terms.d: Option that sends a single email per incident instead of one for every update.
Filter in action notification rules: Completed and/or Failed response actions.

lessons.trap: Candidates confuse these with Sentinel automation rules or the endpoint-only vulnerability notifications; incident, action and threat analytics emails are all under Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Email notifications.
lessons.example: A SOC manager creates an incident rule for High severity only, ticks 'one notification per incident' and adds the on-call distribution list, then sends a test email.

lessons.title: Alert tuning (formerly alert suppression)
lessons.short: **Alert tuning** rules automatically hide or resolve alerts that match conditions you define, such as a known scanner process. They reduce queue noise but can hide real threats if too broad, so keep conditions specific.
lessons.deep:
Alert tuning (previously called **alert suppression**) is configured in **Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Alert tuning**, or straight from an alert's details page (which pre-fills conditions from the alert's evidence).

A rule chooses **service sources** (for example Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Office 365) and then conditions based on **evidence/IOC types** such as file, process, scheduled task, AMSI script or WMI event. Conditions can be combined with **AND/OR** and grouping; up to 200 conditions per rule; values are not case-sensitive and some support wildcards.

Actions:
- **Hide alert**: suppresses the alert so no incident is created; data stays in `AlertInfo` and `AlertEvidence`. Defender for Endpoint alerts only.
- **Resolve alert**: the alert (and related incident) is created but auto-resolved.
- **Set as behavior**: turns matches into behaviors kept for hunting.

Microsoft also ships **built-in tuning rules** for common benign noise; they do not apply to custom detections, and you can disable them. Example: the built-in rule that auto-resolves user-reported phish stops the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent from classifying those alerts. In Unified RBAC, managing tuning needs **Detection tuning (manage)**.

terms.d: Tuning action that suppresses a Defender for Endpoint alert; no incident is created but the data stays in AlertInfo/AlertEvidence.
Tuning action that lets the alert be created but resolves it automatically.
Unified RBAC permission to manage custom detections, alert tuning and indicators.

lessons.trap: Alert tuning is not an exclusion: the activity still happens and is still logged; the exam may offer AV exclusions or automation folder exclusions as wrong ways to cut alert noise.
lessons.example: A nightly vulnerability scanner triggers 'suspicious process' alerts; the team creates a tuning rule matching that scanner process on the scanning server with the Resolve alert action.

lessons.title: Alert correlation and incident merging
lessons.short: Defender XDR **correlates** related alerts from all its products (and the primary Sentinel workspace) into one **incident**, and keeps **merging** incidents that share entities, artifacts or attack sequences. Admins can exclude specific Sentinel analytics rules from correlation.
lessons.deep:
**Correlation** groups alerts that are related within a time frame (same users, devices, mailboxes, files, processes, or a recognisable attack chain) into a single incident. Only the **primary** Sentinel workspace correlates with Defender alerts; secondary workspaces don't.

**Merging**: when two incidents turn out to be related, Defender moves alerts, entities and tags from the source incident to the target. The source is closed and tagged **Redirected**. Defender picks the merge direction.

Automatic merging is blocked when one incident is **closed**, they're **assigned to different people**, they have **different classifications/determinations**, the merge would exceed the entity limit, or (if enabled) devices are in different device groups. You can fix the blocker and merge manually (up to five incidents at once).

To keep a Sentinel analytics rule out of correlation, set **Incident correlation** to *Disabled* in the rule wizard's Incident settings, which adds `#DONT_CORR#` to the start of the rule description (`#INC_CORR#` includes it). This needs Microsoft Sentinel Contributor.

For Defender for Endpoint, the advanced feature **Restrict correlation to within scoped device groups** stops alerts from different device groups being joined, useful for local SOCs.

terms.d: Automatic grouping of related alerts from different sources into one incident.
Tag at the start of a Sentinel analytics rule description that excludes the rule from Defender XDR correlation.
Tag on a source incident that was merged into another and closed.

lessons.trap: Turning off alert grouping in a Sentinel rule does not stop Defender XDR correlation; the exam answer is the Incident correlation setting / #DONT_CORR# tag.
lessons.example: A phishing email alert and a later malicious-file alert on the recipient's laptop are correlated into one multi-stage incident.

lessons.title: Defender for Endpoint advanced features
lessons.short: **Advanced features** are tenant-wide on/off switches in Settings > Endpoints > Advanced features, such as EDR in block mode, tamper protection, custom network indicators, live response, and integrations with Intune, Defender for Cloud Apps and Purview.
lessons.deep:
Go to **Settings > Endpoints > Advanced features**, toggle On/Off and select **Save preferences**. Exam-relevant switches:
- **Restrict correlation to within scoped device groups**: local SOCs only see incidents for their device groups (affects future correlation only).
- **Enable EDR in block mode**: EDR blocks malicious artifacts even when Defender Antivirus runs in **passive mode**.
- **Automatically resolve alerts**: resolves alerts where no threats were found or threats were remediated.
- **Allow or block file**: needed to block files by indicator; requires Defender Antivirus as the **active** antimalware and **cloud-based protection** on.
- **Custom network indicators**: allow/block IPs, domains and URLs from your indicator list.
- **Tamper protection**: stops apps and users changing Defender security settings.
- **Web content filtering**, **Device discovery**, **Show user details**.
- **Live response**, **Live response for servers**, **Allow unsigned script execution in live response** (each separate).
- **Download quarantined files** (on by default).
- **Microsoft Intune connection** (device risk for Conditional Access), **Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps**, **Share endpoint alerts with Microsoft Purview** (insider risk).
- **Hide potential duplicate device records** (on by default).

terms.d: Lets Defender for Endpoint EDR block threats even when a non-Microsoft AV is primary and Defender AV is passive.
Locks Defender Antivirus settings so malware or users cannot turn protection off.
Separate switch that allows live response sessions on server operating systems.

lessons.trap: Live response, live response for servers and unsigned script execution are three separate switches; enabling one does not enable the others.
lessons.example: A company running a third-party AV turns on EDR in block mode so Defender for Endpoint can still remediate post-breach detections.

lessons.title: Rules settings: indicators of compromise
lessons.short: Under Settings > Endpoints > Rules > **Indicators** you define **IoCs** (file hashes, IPs, URLs/domains, certificates) with an action such as Allow, Audit, Warn, Block execution or Block and remediate, scoped to device groups.
lessons.deep:
The **Rules** section of Defender for Endpoint settings holds rule-type configuration: **Indicators**, automation uploads, automation folder exclusions, web content filtering and custom data collection.

**Indicators of compromise (IoCs)** let you decide how specific entities are treated. For each indicator you set the **action**, an expiry and the **device groups** in scope:
- **Files** (hash): Allow, Audit, Warn, Block execution, Block and remediate.
- **IP addresses** and **URLs/domains**: Allow, Audit, Warn, Block execution.
- **Certificates** (.CER/.PEM): Allow, Block and remediate.

Notes: limit of **15,000 indicators per tenant** (cannot be increased). IP indicators need full IPv4/IPv6 addresses (no CIDR ranges or wildcards). A domain indicator also matches subdomains. Indicators are not supported when Defender Antivirus is in **passive mode**, and Microsoft-signed apps can't be blocked. File indicators require the **Allow or block file** advanced feature; IP/URL indicators require **Custom network indicators**. **Audit** raises an alert at the severity you choose; **Warn** shows a bypassable prompt. Managing indicators needs Unified RBAC **Detection tuning** (or Response for automation allow/block lists).

terms.d: Indicator of compromise: a file hash, IP, URL/domain or certificate with a defined action.
Indicator action for files/certificates that blocks and also removes the item.
Indicator action that shows the user a warning they can bypass.

lessons.trap: Block and remediate is not available for IP or URL indicators, and IP indicators cannot take a CIDR range.
lessons.example: During an incident the SOC adds the attacker's C2 domain as a Block execution indicator for all device groups.

lessons.title: Rules settings: automation uploads and folder exclusions
lessons.short: **Automation uploads** controls which file types are sent to the cloud for deeper inspection during automated investigation (Content analysis). **Automation folder exclusions** tell automated investigation to skip specific folders, while antivirus still scans them.
lessons.deep:
Two Defender for Endpoint settings tune how automated investigation treats files.

**Automation uploads** (Settings > Endpoints > Rules > Automation uploads): turn **Content analysis** On/Off and list file extension names (comma-separated, for example `exe,bat`). Matching suspicious files are uploaded for cloud inspection during automated investigation. Submitted files are kept for six months.

**Automation folder exclusions**: add a **folder** (required; includes subfolders, trailing wildcard allowed), optional **extensions** and **file names**, and a **description**. Automated investigation ignores excluded items, and live response attempts to collect those files fail with *File is excluded*. Exclusions apply to all onboarded devices and affect **only automated investigation**; antivirus still scans the files. Specify file names where possible so attackers can't hide in an excluded folder.

Permissions: Unified RBAC **Core security settings (manage)**, or Security Administrator. Not available in Defender for Business.

terms.d: Automation uploads toggle that sends selected file types to the cloud for inspection during automated investigation.
Folder that automated investigation skips; antivirus scanning still applies.

lessons.trap: Automation folder exclusions are not antivirus exclusions; they only stop automated investigation from examining the folder.
lessons.example: A build server folder full of compiled test binaries keeps generating investigations, so the team excludes the folder for named build outputs only.

lessons.title: Custom data collection in Defender for Endpoint
lessons.short: **Custom data collection** rules gather extra endpoint events beyond default telemetry, filtered by paths, process names or connections, from devices chosen by **dynamic tags**, and send them to a connected **Microsoft Sentinel** workspace in `DeviceCustom*` tables.
lessons.deep:
Default Defender for Endpoint telemetry is sampled and summarised. When you need more (for example every PowerShell launch on admin workstations), create a **custom data collection rule** at **Settings > Endpoints > Rules > Custom Data Collection**.

**Prerequisites**: Defender for Endpoint **Plan 2**; a connected **Microsoft Sentinel workspace** (currently one per tenant) selected in the rule wizard; **dynamic tags** created in **Asset rule management** (manual tags are not supported); Windows 10/11 or Windows Server 2019+.

**Steps**: choose the workspace, Create rule (name), choose the **table**, actions and conditions, define **scope** (all devices or dynamic tags), review and submit. Rules deploy in about 20 minutes to 1 hour.

**Tables** in Sentinel: `DeviceCustomProcessEvents`, `DeviceCustomFileEvents`, `DeviceCustomNetworkEvents`, `DeviceCustomScriptEvents`, `DeviceCustomImageLoadEvents`. Each row has a **RuleName** column; use `TimeGenerated` for time.

**Limits and cost**: each rule collects up to **75,000 events per device per 24-hour rolling window**; then that rule pauses on that device while other rules continue. The feature is included in Plan 2, but **Sentinel ingestion is billed**.

terms.d: Sentinel table holding process events gathered by custom data collection rules.
Device tag assigned automatically by Asset rule management rules; required to target custom collection.
Column showing which custom collection rule captured the event.

lessons.trap: Custom collection data goes to the Sentinel workspace (DeviceCustom* tables), not to the standard Device* tables, and it needs dynamic, not manual, tags.
lessons.example: To meet a PCI audit, the team collects all file modifications in a cardholder-data folder on tagged servers into DeviceCustomFileEvents.

lessons.title: Endpoint security policies in the Defender portal
lessons.short: With **security settings management**, you create Defender for Endpoint **endpoint security policies** (antivirus, firewall, EDR, ASR rules and more) directly in the Defender portal and assign them to Microsoft Entra groups, even for devices not enrolled in Intune.
lessons.deep:
The **Endpoint security policies** page in the Defender portal uses the same policy engine as Intune. Before you can use it you must connect Intune and Defender for Endpoint and enable **security settings management**.

Policy types include **Microsoft Defender Antivirus**, **Antivirus exclusions**, **Microsoft Defender Firewall** and **Firewall rules**, **Endpoint detection and response (EDR)**, **Attack surface reduction (ASR) rules**, **Device control** and **Windows Security experience**. Windows supports all; macOS and Linux support Antivirus and EDR.

Create a policy: **Create new policy** > choose platform and template > **Basics** (name) > **Configuration settings** > **Assignments** (include/exclude groups) > **Review + create**.

Assignment uses Microsoft **Entra security groups**. Devices managed only by security settings management (not Intune-enrolled) must be targeted with **device groups**; user targeting isn't supported for them. Such devices check in every **90 minutes**; force it with **More actions > Policy sync** on the device page.

Permissions: a role that applies to all devices, such as Unified RBAC **Core security settings**, Intune **Endpoint Security Manager**, or Security Administrator.

terms.d: Feature that lets Defender-onboarded devices receive Intune endpoint security policies without full Intune enrollment.
Device action that forces an immediate check-in for endpoint security policies.

lessons.trap: Defender-only managed devices cannot be targeted with user groups; policies must go to Entra groups containing the devices.
lessons.example: A Linux server fleet gets an EDR policy from the Defender portal without being enrolled in Intune.

lessons.title: Attack surface reduction (ASR) rules
lessons.short: **ASR rules** block risky behaviours malware uses, such as Office spawning child processes or credential theft from LSASS. Each rule can be Not configured, **Block**, **Audit** or **Warn**. Test in Audit first, then Block.
lessons.deep:
Attack surface reduction rules target behaviours rather than signatures. Each rule has a GUID and a mode:
- **Not configured / Disabled** (`0`)
- **Block** (`1`): behaviour is stopped and logged.
- **Audit** (`2`): behaviour is allowed but logged, for impact testing.
- **Warn** (`6`): user sees a block they can bypass. Not supported by *Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem* or *Block Office applications from injecting code into other processes*.

Microsoft's **standard protection rules** (block vulnerable signed drivers, block LSASS credential stealing, block WMI persistence) are the minimum set to enable broadly.

Deploy via **endpoint security ASR policy** (Defender portal or Intune), Configuration Manager, Group Policy, or PowerShell, e.g. `Add-MpPreference -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids <GUID> -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions 2`.

Monitor in **Reports > Attack surface reduction rules** (Detections, Configuration, Add exclusions tabs) and in advanced hunting: `DeviceEvents | where ActionType startswith "Asr"` (for example `AsrLsassCredentialTheftAudited` / `...Blocked`). Exclusions can be global or per rule; switch a suspected false positive to Audit before excluding.

terms.d: ASR mode that logs what would have been blocked without blocking it.
ASR mode that blocks but lets the user choose to unblock.
Microsoft's recommended baseline ASR rules to enable on almost all devices.

lessons.trap: The LSASS credential-theft rule has no Warn mode, and ASR events are in DeviceEvents (ActionType starting 'Asr'), not in a dedicated ASR table.
lessons.example: Before blocking 'Block all Office applications from creating child processes', an admin runs it in Audit for two weeks and reviews DeviceEvents for business macros.

lessons.title: Automated investigation and response (AIR)
lessons.short: **AIR** investigates alerts like a tier-1 analyst, gives each piece of evidence a verdict (Malicious, Suspicious, No threats found) and either remediates automatically or queues actions for approval in the **Action center**.
lessons.deep:
When an alert starts an automated investigation, AIR examines related entities across devices (Defender for Endpoint), email and content (Defender for Office 365) and on-premises identities (Defender for Identity). Each item gets a verdict: **Malicious**, **Suspicious** or **No threats found**. Remediation actions (quarantine file, stop process, isolate device, soft-delete email, block URL) run automatically or wait for approval depending on configuration; for devices that's the **device group automation level**.

The **Action center** (security.microsoft.com/action-center) has **Pending** (approve/reject) and **History** (audit log of automated and manual actions, live response commands and AV remediations; some actions such as **Isolate device** can be **undone**). Email remediation from AIR is never automatic; it always waits for approval.

Approving: Unified RBAC **Response (manage)** for devices; **Email & collaboration advanced actions (manage)** for email (or Security Administrator plus Search and Purge).

**2026 change**: from **September 1, 2026**, AIR in Defender for Endpoint no longer runs as a separate investigation experience and can't be triggered manually; its capabilities run inside default antivirus protection. Use a **full antivirus scan** for on-demand investigation. AIR for Defender for Office 365 continues.

terms.d: Single place to approve pending remediation actions and review/undo completed ones.
AIR's judgement on evidence: Malicious, Suspicious or No threats found.

lessons.trap: Email remediation found by AIR is never fully automatic; it always needs approval in the Action center.
lessons.example: An automated investigation finds a malicious attachment in 40 mailboxes; the analyst approves the pending soft-delete action in the Action center.

lessons.title: Automatic attack disruption
lessons.short: **Automatic attack disruption** spots high-confidence attacks in progress (ransomware, BEC, AiTM) and automatically contains attacker-controlled assets, for example containing devices or disabling users, to stop lateral movement while analysts investigate.
lessons.deep:
Attack disruption works at incident level using correlated XDR signals. Actions include **Contain device**, **Isolate device**, **Contain IP** and **Contain user** (Defender for Endpoint), **Disable user in AD** (Defender for Identity, via the sensor on a domain controller), **Disable/suspend user in Entra ID**, **Revoke user session**, and protection against **OAuth app compromise** (Defender for Cloud Apps).

**Prerequisites**: Device discovery set to **Standard discovery** (for Contain device); device groups at **Full** automation recommended (Semi still allows disruption); Defender for Identity sensors on DCs with auditing configured; the Defender for Cloud Apps **Microsoft 365 connector with all checkboxes**; Exchange Online mailboxes with audit. It works whatever the Defender Antivirus state (active, passive, EDR block mode).

**Exclusions** (not recommended): **Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Automated response**: **Identities** tab > Add user exclusion (e.g. break-glass, service accounts); **Devices** tab for device groups (automation level **No automated response**) and **Exclude IP**.

**Seeing and undoing**: incidents get the **Attack Disruption** tag and a yellow banner; actions appear in the Action center. Select the asset and choose **Release from containment** or **Enable user**.

terms.d: Defender for Endpoint action that blocks a compromised account's communication and authentication from onboarded devices.
Tag added to incidents where automatic disruption took action.
Settings page where users, device groups and IPs are excluded from disruption.

lessons.trap: Excluding an account from disruption is done in Defender XDR Automated response settings, not with a Conditional Access exclusion or alert tuning.
lessons.example: During a ransomware attack, disruption disables the compromised domain admin in AD and contains the encrypting servers before files on other hosts are touched.

lessons.title: Device groups and permissions in Defender for Endpoint
lessons.short: **Device groups** sort devices by matching rules (name, domain, tag, OS). They control **who can see which devices** (via Entra user groups and roles) and which **automation level** applies. A device belongs only to its highest-ranked matching group.
lessons.deep:
Create device groups at **Settings > Endpoints > Permissions > Device groups**. Each group has:
- **General**: unique name, **automation (remediation) level**, description.
- **Devices**: matching rule on **device name, domain, tags, OS platform**. All specified conditions must match; multiple rows of the same property are ORed.
- **Preview devices**.
- **User access**: Microsoft Entra user groups that already have roles.

**Rank** decides membership: rank 1 is highest and a device joins only the **highest-ranked** group it matches. **Ungrouped devices (default)** catches the rest; it can't be deleted or re-ranked, but you can change its automation level and access.

A group with no assigned user groups is visible to all portal users. Tags (manual, registry `DeviceTagging\Group`, Intune, API or dynamic rules) drive membership.

**Permissions**: Microsoft Defender XDR **Unified RBAC** is now the default (new tenants since February 2025, with remaining tenants being auto-enabled from late 2026). Custom roles combine permissions such as **Security data basics (read)**, **Alerts (manage)**, **Response (manage)**, **Basic/Advanced live response**, **Detection tuning**, **Authorization** (manage device groups and roles), and are scoped to device groups. In legacy MDE RBAC, turning RBAC on was irreversible.

terms.d: Priority order; a device joins only the highest-ranked group whose rule it matches.
Built-in catch-all group that can't be deleted or re-ranked.
Single Defender XDR permission model across Defender workloads and Sentinel, with device-group scoping.

lessons.trap: A device that matches two groups is not in both; it goes only to the higher-ranked group.
lessons.example: A 'DE-Servers' group matches tag DE and OS Windows Server, ranked above 'All-Servers', and only the German SOC's Entra group has access to it.

lessons.title: Automation levels for device groups
lessons.short: Each device group's **automation level** decides whether AIR remediations run automatically or need approval: Full, three Semi levels (all folders, core folders, non-temp folders), or No automated response. Microsoft recommends **Full**.
lessons.deep:
The levels, from most to least automated:
- **Full - remediate threats automatically**: remediation runs on malicious entities; actions show in Action center History and can be undone. Recommended, and the default for tenants created on or after 16 August 2020.
- **Semi - require approval for core folders remediation**: approval only for files in **core folders** (operating system directories such as `\windows\*`); other folders auto-remediate.
- **Semi - require approval for non-temp folders remediation**: only files in **temporary folders** (e.g. `\users\*\appdata\local\temp\*`, `\windows\temp\*`, Downloads) auto-remediate; everything else needs approval.
- **Semi - require approval for all folders**: every remediation waits on the Pending tab (default for tenants created before 16 August 2020).
- **No automated response**: automated investigation doesn't run. Not recommended; also excludes the group from attack disruption device actions.

Pending actions not approved time out after seven days. Set the level per device group, including **Ungrouped devices (default)**.

terms.d: Operating system directories such as \windows\*.
Remediation actions on malicious entities run without approval.

lessons.trap: 'Core folders' means OS folders, and 'non-temp folders' is the stricter Semi level: only temp-folder files are fixed automatically.
lessons.example: Domain controllers are placed in a group with 'Semi - require approval for core folders remediation' so no system files are changed without review.

lessons.title: Microsoft Sentinel automation rules
lessons.short: **Automation rules** centrally automate incident and alert handling in Sentinel: a **trigger** (incident created, incident updated, alert created), **conditions**, and ordered **actions** such as change status/severity, assign owner, add tags or tasks, or **run playbook**.
lessons.deep:
Automation rules are lightweight SOAR without code.

**Triggers**: **When incident is created**; **When incident is updated** (status, owner, severity, alerts, comments, tags, tactics change); **When alert is created** (Scheduled/NRT rules; mainly for rules that don't create incidents).

**Conditions**: incident properties (including analytics rule name, entities) with operators like equals, contains, starts with. Update triggers add **Updated by** (user, application, AIR, alert grouping/Defender XDR correlation, playbook, automation rule) and state-change operators (changed, changed to). Conditions see the **current state**: if an earlier rule lowered severity, later rules see the new value.

**Actions** (run in listed order): change status (close with reason and comment), change severity, assign owner, add tags, **add task**, **run playbook** (incident rules run incident-trigger playbooks; alert rules run alert-trigger playbooks).

**Order**: rules run **sequentially, never in parallel**, by order number; duplicate numbers run in random order. Optional **expiration** date auto-disables a rule (handy for pen-test suppression). Rules can be created from the Automation page, the analytics rule wizard, or an incident (pre-filled suppression).

To run playbooks, the **Sentinel service account** needs permissions on the playbook's resource group.

terms.d: Sentinel rule with trigger, conditions and actions that runs sequentially by order number.
Update-trigger condition identifying who changed the incident, used to avoid automation loops.
Date after which an automation rule is disabled automatically.

lessons.trap: Automation rules run one at a time in order, and each sees the incident as changed by earlier rules.
lessons.example: A rule closes incidents from the 'Pen test sign-ins' analytics rule as Benign Positive and expires at the end of the test week.

lessons.title: Microsoft Sentinel playbooks
lessons.short: **Playbooks** are **Azure Logic Apps** workflows that Sentinel runs on an incident, alert or entity, automatically through automation rules or manually, for enrichment, ticketing, notifications and response such as disabling a user.
lessons.deep:
A playbook is a Logic App that starts from a Microsoft Sentinel connector **trigger**: **incident** (receives the incident with its alerts and entities, called a *case* in the Defender portal), **alert**, or **entity** (run manually during investigation or hunting).

**Use cases**: enrichment (IP reputation), bi-directional sync with ServiceNow, orchestration (post to Teams), response (block an account, isolate a device).

**Consumption vs Standard**: Consumption runs in multi-tenant Logic Apps and supports Sentinel **playbook templates** (from the Automation page or Content hub). **Standard** runs single-tenant, supports **private endpoints and VNet integration**, but can't be created from templates and Sentinel doesn't support **stateless** Standard workflows.

**Authentication** to Sentinel: managed identity (recommended), service principal, or user. Give the managed identity **Microsoft Sentinel Responder** to update incidents, or **Reader** if it only receives them.

**Roles**: **Logic App Contributor** to build/edit; **Microsoft Sentinel Playbook Operator** to run manually; the Sentinel service account needs **Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor** on the playbook's resource group so automation rules can call it (granted via **Manage playbook permissions**, which needs Owner).

terms.d: Azure Logic Apps workflow triggered by Sentinel on an incident, alert or entity.
Azure identity for the logic app, granted a Sentinel role so it can call Sentinel without stored credentials.
Role for the Sentinel service account so automation rules can run playbooks; not for users.

lessons.trap: If a playbook doesn't appear in an automation rule, the fix is granting Sentinel permissions on the playbook's resource group, not giving the analyst Logic App Contributor.
lessons.example: An incident-trigger playbook with a managed identity enriches IP entities with threat intel and posts the incident summary to a Teams channel.

lessons.title: Microsoft Sentinel roles
lessons.short: Sentinel uses Azure RBAC built-in roles: **Reader** (view), **Responder** (view + manage incidents), **Contributor** (+ create rules, workbooks, content hub), plus **Playbook Operator** and **Automation Contributor**. Assign at resource-group scope with least privilege.
lessons.deep:
Built-in Azure roles for the Sentinel SIEM:
- **Microsoft Sentinel Reader**: view data, incidents, workbooks and recommendations.
- **Microsoft Sentinel Responder**: Reader + manage incidents (assign, change status, dismiss).
- **Microsoft Sentinel Contributor**: Responder + create/edit analytics rules, workbooks and other content; install/update solutions in **Content hub**.
- **Microsoft Sentinel Playbook Operator**: list, view and manually run playbooks.
- **Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor**: lets Sentinel add playbooks to automation rules; **not for user accounts**.

Companion roles: **Logic App Contributor** (build playbooks), **Workbook Contributor** (needed with Reader/Responder to save workbooks), **Log Analytics Reader/Contributor**. Roles are **cumulative**. Microsoft's guidance: SOC analysts = Responder + Playbook Operator; security engineers = Contributor + Logic App Contributor. Guest users assigned incidents also need Entra **Directory Reader**.

The **Sentinel data lake** uses **Microsoft Entra roles**: Global Reader, Security Reader, Security Operator, Security Administrator and Global Administrator can read; only **Security Operator**, Security Administrator and Global Administrator can write (KQL jobs, notebooks) or manage scheduled jobs.

In the Defender portal, **Unified RBAC** can also grant Sentinel workspace access (it syncs with Azure RBAC).

terms.d: Role that adds incident management (assign, status, dismiss) on top of Reader.
Role that can create and edit analytics rules, workbooks and content hub solutions.
Role that can run but not edit playbooks.

lessons.trap: Automation Contributor is never the answer for a human user; it's for the Sentinel service account.
lessons.example: Tier-1 analysts get Microsoft Sentinel Responder on the Sentinel resource group and Playbook Operator on the playbooks' resource group.

lessons.title: Data tiers and retention: Analytics vs Data lake
lessons.short: Sentinel tables live in the **Analytics tier** (hot, all features, 30 days to 2 years) or the **Data lake tier** (cheap, long-term, up to 12 years total, queried with KQL jobs and notebooks). Manage both per table in Microsoft Sentinel > Configuration > **Tables**.
lessons.deep:
**Analytics tier**: full-feature storage for analytics rules, hunting, workbooks, watchlists and real-time queries. Analytics retention can be set from **30 days to 2 years**; Sentinel-enabled workspaces include **90 days** of retention at no extra charge.

**Data lake tier**: low-cost storage for data you don't need for real-time detection (high-volume firewall, proxy, audit or compliance logs). Query it with **KQL jobs**, scheduled jobs, **summary rules** and **notebooks**. It is **not** available to analytics rules, hunting queries, watchlists or workbooks.

By default analytics data is **mirrored** to the data lake, and **total retention** can extend to **12 years**. A table can also be set to **Data lake tier** only.

Manage in the Defender portal: **Microsoft Sentinel > Configuration > Tables**, select a table, **Manage table**, choose tier, analytics retention and total retention. Needs Unified RBAC **Data (manage)** or Log Analytics Contributor-level workspace rights.

Behaviour: analytics retention changes apply immediately; shortening total retention waits 30 days; increasing it applies to existing data. Moving Analytics → Data lake stops rules and hunting on that table. Basic Logs tables can be viewed but are managed in the Log Analytics workspace.

terms.d: Hot storage supporting all Sentinel features; 30 days to 2 years retention.
Low-cost long-term storage (total retention up to 12 years) queried by KQL jobs and notebooks.
Analytics retention plus data lake retention for a table.

lessons.trap: Data that analytics rules or workbooks must use cannot sit only in the data lake tier.
lessons.example: Firewall traffic logs are set to Data lake tier with 1-year total retention, while SigninLogs stay in Analytics for 180 days.

lessons.title: Retention for Defender XDR tables
lessons.short: Defender XDR advanced hunting tables (e.g. `DeviceProcessEvents`) keep **30 days** by default at no extra cost. With Sentinel onboarded to the Defender portal you can extend them in Table management, in the Analytics tier or straight to the **Data lake tier**.
lessons.deep:
The **XDR default tier** holds advanced hunting data for **30 days**, included with the Defender licence. (Defender for Endpoint keeps its own portal data such as timelines for 180 days, but **advanced hunting queries reach back 30 days**.)

To keep XDR data longer, onboard Microsoft Sentinel to the Defender portal, then in **Microsoft Sentinel > Configuration > Tables** set retention above 30 days for supported XDR tables:
- **Analytics tier** (e.g. 90 or 180 days): the data is ingested into Sentinel, so **Sentinel ingestion costs apply**; storage up to 90 days is included.
- **Data lake tier only**: avoids analytics ingestion cost; the first 30 days remain in advanced hunting at no extra cost, and older data is queried with KQL jobs or notebooks.

Resetting both analytics and total retention back to 30 days stops analytics-tier ingestion for that table. Some XDR and solution tables must stay in the Analytics tier because Microsoft services need them for near-real-time detection.

Table types shown in the portal: **Microsoft Sentinel** tables, **Custom** tables (`_CL`, also summary rule and search job results), and **XDR** tables (view-only until managed).

terms.d: Built-in 30-day advanced hunting retention included with Defender licences.
Defender portal page (Sentinel > Configuration > Tables) to set tier and retention per table.

lessons.trap: Extending XDR tables in the Analytics tier costs Sentinel ingestion; choosing Data lake tier avoids that but loses real-time analytics on the older data.
lessons.example: To hunt a dwell-time of four months, a SOC sets DeviceNetworkEvents to 180 days analytics retention.

lessons.title: Microsoft Sentinel workbooks
lessons.short: **Workbooks** are interactive dashboards built on Azure Monitor workbooks. Install templates from **Content hub**, save them to **My workbooks**, then edit by adding text, KQL queries and **parameters** such as a time range.
lessons.deep:
Workbooks visualise Sentinel data with charts, grids and tiles. Each saved workbook is an **Azure resource** in the workspace's resource group, so access uses Azure RBAC: at least **Workbook Reader** to view, **Workbook Contributor** to create/edit (Sentinel Contributor includes it).

**From a template**: install the solution in **Content hub** (e.g. Microsoft Entra solution for the sign-in and audit logs workbooks), go to **Workbooks > Templates**, check **Required data types**, **Save**, then **View saved workbook** and **Edit**. Saving stores only the JSON definition, not data. Templates can't be deleted.

**From scratch**: **Add workbook** > **Edit** > add text, queries (data source **Logs**, resource type **Log Analytics**) and parameters > **Done editing** > **Save**. Microsoft recommends **ASIM parsers** so a workbook works across data sources.

**Parameters**: a time range parameter is referenced in KQL as `{TimeRange}` (expands to e.g. `> ago(1d)`), with `{TimeRange:start}`, `{TimeRange:end}` and `{TimeRange:grain}` for `make-series`.

**Auto refresh** can be 5 minutes to 1 day (off by default). Workbooks can't query data-lake-only tables.

terms.d: Read-only workbook installed from Content hub; save it to create your own copy.
Workbook time parameter placeholder used in KQL filters.
Azure role needed (with Reader/Responder) to save or edit workbooks.

lessons.trap: A Sentinel Reader or Responder can view workbooks but needs Workbook Contributor to save one.
lessons.example: An engineer saves the 'Microsoft Entra sign-in logs' template, adds a parameter for country and a TimeRange picker, and shares it with the SOC.

lessons.title: SOC optimization recommendations
lessons.short: **SOC optimization** in the Defender portal gives tailored recommendations to get more value from ingested data (**data value**), close detection gaps (**threat-based / risk-based coverage**, AI MITRE tagging) and add data sources that **similar organizations** use.
lessons.deep:
SOC optimization requires a Sentinel workspace **onboarded to the Defender portal** and standard Sentinel roles. Recommendations are recalculated every **24 hours**.

**Types**:
- **Data value**: for billable tables with data in the last 30 days. If a table isn't used by any analytics rule but is used by workbooks/hunting, turn on rule templates or move it to a cheaper plan; if it's unused entirely, enable templates or stop ingesting it. Tables used for UEBA or TI matching are left alone.
- **Threat-based coverage**: compares your data and rules to what's needed against attacks such as ransomware or AiTM. Data present but detections missing → turn on analytics rule templates; rules on but data missing → connect data sources.
- **Risk-based coverage** (preview) and **AI MITRE ATT&CK tagging** (preview, suggests tactics/techniques for untagged rules).
- **Similar organizations**: tables missing from your workspace that comparable organisations ingest (excludes custom tables, Syslog/CommonSecurityLog).

**States**: Active, In progress (*Mark as in progress*), Completed (manual or automatic), Dismissed. Actions: View details, **Go to Content Hub**, Change plan, provide feedback, reactivate. The overview shows data ingested (90 days) and threat coverage levels (High >75%, Medium, Low).

terms.d: Suggests using or reducing ingested tables that give little detection value.
Recommendation that maps data and rules against specific attack scenarios.

lessons.trap: When the data exists but detections are missing, the recommendation is to enable analytics rule templates, not to connect more data.
lessons.example: SOC optimization shows the AiTM scenario at Low coverage because Entra sign-in data is present but the matching rule templates are off.

lessons.title: Optimizing Sentinel cost and health
lessons.short: Optimize the platform by watching **ingestion** (the `Usage` table), choosing a pricing plan (**commitment tiers** from 100 GB/day), using free data sources, and monitoring automation and connectors with the **SentinelHealth** table.
lessons.deep:
**Measure ingestion** with the `Usage` table: `Quantity` is in **MB**, `IsBillable` marks billable data, `DataType` is the table, `Solution` the source solution (SecurityInsights = Sentinel). Summing `Quantity` by `DataType` shows which tables cost most.

**Pricing**: pay-as-you-go by default, or **commitment tiers** starting at **100 GB/day** for a discount. You can raise the tier any time but lower it only once every **31 days**. Free sources include **AzureActivity**, **OfficeActivity** (Office 365 audit), **SentinelHealth**, and Defender alerts/incidents (**SecurityAlert**, **SecurityIncident**). Analytics data is retained free for 90 days.

Other levers: move verbose tables to the data lake tier, filter with DCR transformations, act on SOC optimization data value recommendations.

**Health**: turn on Sentinel **health monitoring** to populate **SentinelHealth**. For automation, `OperationName` is *Automation rule run* (Status Success, Partial success, Failure) or *Playbook was triggered*. Playbook run details need Logic Apps diagnostic settings sending to the workspace (**AzureDiagnostics**).

terms.d: Hourly ingestion volume per table; Quantity in MB.
Discounted fixed daily ingestion level from 100 GB/day; decrease once every 31 days.
Table recording health events for connectors, analytics rules and automation.

lessons.trap: Usage.Quantity is in megabytes, not bytes or GB; divide by 1000 for GB.
lessons.example: A weekly query on Usage shows CommonSecurityLog is 60% of cost, so the team filters noisy firewall events with a DCR transformation.

lessons.title: Choosing data connectors
lessons.short: Data connectors bring logs into the Log Analytics workspace behind Microsoft Sentinel. Most arrive as Content hub solutions. Pick a connector by source type: service-to-service (Microsoft services), diagnostic settings (Azure resources), agent-based via the Azure Monitor Agent (servers and appliances), or API-based (third-party SaaS).
lessons.deep:
Microsoft Sentinel is only as good as the data it sees. A **data connector** is the packaged method for getting one source's logs into the workspace, and it usually installs as part of a **Content hub** solution that also brings analytics rules, workbooks and playbooks.

The main families:
- **Service-to-service**: Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft 365. Mostly a few clicks, but they need tenant roles (for example Security Administrator) plus write access on the workspace.
- **Diagnostic settings-based**: Azure resources send logs through a diagnostic setting, sometimes deployed at scale by **Azure Policy**.
- **Agent-based (AMA)**: the **Azure Monitor Agent** with a **data collection rule (DCR)** collects Windows events, Syslog, CEF and text files.
- **API-based**: the **Codeless Connector Framework (CCF)** polls or receives pushed data. Push connectors use the **Logs Ingestion API** (a DCR plus an Entra app).

Licensing matters too. The Entra ID connector needs Entra ID P1 or P2 for sign-in logs, though audit logs work with any licence.

For exam scenarios, read the source first (Azure resource, on-premises server, firewall, SaaS app). Then match the transport (policy, AMA, API) and check the destination table.

terms.d: Packaged configuration that ingests one data source's logs into the Sentinel workspace.
Sentinel catalogue where solutions (connectors, rules, workbooks, playbooks) are installed.
Microsoft framework for building API polling or push connectors without hosting code.
Azure Monitor REST API that sends data through a DCR to a workspace table.

lessons.trap: Candidates pick an agent connector for an Azure PaaS service. Azure resources use diagnostic settings or Azure Policy, not AMA.
lessons.example: A SOC must ingest Entra ID sign-ins, Azure Key Vault logs and a Palo Alto firewall. That calls for three paths: the Entra ID connector, diagnostic settings via Azure Policy, and CEF via AMA.

lessons.title: Windows log connector choices
lessons.short: For Windows, Windows Security Events via AMA writes to SecurityEvent, the table most built-in rules query. Windows Forwarded Events reads the WEF collector's ForwardedEvents channel and writes to WindowsEvent. Defender XDR's connector can stream endpoint advanced hunting tables such as DeviceProcessEvents.
lessons.deep:
There are three common ways to get Windows activity into Microsoft Sentinel. The destination table decides which built-in content will work.

- **Windows Security Events via AMA**: the AMA runs on each server, Azure VM or **Azure Arc-enabled** machine. It collects the Security log (and AppLocker) into the **SecurityEvent** table. Many built-in analytics rules, including some NRT rules, query this table.
- **Windows Forwarded Events**: you build a **Windows Event Forwarding (WEF)** setup in which sources push events to a **Windows Event Collector (WEC)** server. The AMA on the WEC reads the forwarded events into the **WindowsEvent** table, even when they came from the Security log. Rules written for SecurityEvent won't match WindowsEvent data unless you adapt them or use ASIM parsers.
- **Microsoft Defender XDR connector**: incidents and alerts, plus optional advanced hunting tables (DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceLogonEvents, DeviceRegistryEvents…) from Defender for Endpoint sensors.

Pick based on the requirement. If you need the out-of-the-box SecurityEvent rules with no edits, use Security Events via AMA. If you must avoid agents on every server, use WEF plus one collector. For EDR telemetry, use Defender XDR.

terms.d: Table filled by the Windows Security Events connectors; queried by many built-in rules.
Table filled by the Windows Forwarded Events connector, whatever the original channel.
Advanced Security Information Model: normalising parsers that let rules work across source tables.

lessons.trap: Forwarded Security log events do NOT land in SecurityEvent. They land in WindowsEvent, so built-in SecurityEvent rules miss them.
lessons.example: Built-in 'SecurityEvent' rules stay silent after a WEF rollout. The analyst finds the data in WindowsEvent and either adapts the queries or deploys Security Events via AMA instead.

lessons.title: Windows Security Events via AMA and DCRs
lessons.short: Windows Security Events via AMA uses a data collection rule (DCR) that names the target machines and the events to collect. You choose an event set (All, Common, Minimal) or Custom XPath queries. Machines outside Azure need Azure Arc first, and the AMA is installed automatically on the selected resources.
lessons.deep:
**Setup flow:** install the Windows Server Security Events solution from the Content hub. Open the **Windows Security Events via AMA** connector, choose **+Add data collection rule**, then:
- **Basics**: DCR name, subscription, resource group. These don't have to match the machines, but they must be in the same tenant.
- **Resources**: select Azure VMs or **Azure Arc-enabled servers**. The AMA is pushed to any that lack it. On-premises or other-cloud servers need the Arc Connected Machine agent *before* this step.
- **Collect**: pick an event set:
  - **All**: the full Security and AppLocker logs (highest volume).
  - **Common**: a full user audit trail at reduced volume (logons, logoffs such as 4634, group changes, Kerberos on DCs).
  - **Minimal**: a small set that may indicate a breach (4624, 4625, 4688, 1102, 4720…). Not a full audit trail.
  - **Custom**: your own **XPath 1.0** queries, e.g. `Security!*[System[(EventID=4624)]]`.

Test an XPath locally with `Get-WinEvent -LogName Security -FilterXPath '…'`. Creating DCRs needs **Monitoring Contributor**, and deploying the agent needs Virtual Machine Contributor or Azure Connected Machine Resource Administrator. For MSSPs, DCRs can also be created by REST API with the `Microsoft-SecurityEvent` stream.

terms.d: Azure Monitor object defining what to collect, from which machines, any transformation, and the destination.
Projects non-Azure servers into Azure Resource Manager so the AMA and DCRs can manage them.
Query syntax (version 1.0 for AMA) that filters Windows events by channel and attributes.
Small, high-value Security event list for breach indicators; no full audit trail.

lessons.trap: 'Install the Log Analytics agent (MMA)' is the outdated answer. AMA plus a DCR is current, and non-Azure servers need Azure Arc.
lessons.example: To cut cost, an admin collects only 4624, 4625 and 4672 from tier-0 servers. They use a Custom DCR with an XPath filter tested first with Get-WinEvent.

lessons.title: Windows Event Forwarding (WEF)
lessons.short: Windows Event Forwarding is built into Windows. Source computers push or are pulled for events over WinRM to a Windows Event Collector (WEC) server, where they land in the ForwardedEvents log. Sentinel then collects that log with the AMA on the WEC via the Windows Forwarded Events connector.
lessons.deep:
**Why use WEF?** It centralises events without an agent on every endpoint. Only the collector runs the AMA.

**Subscription types:**
- **Source-initiated (push)**: Group Policy points clients at the collector using **Configure target Subscription Manager** (Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Event Forwarding). It scales best and suits large fleets. The subscription ACL lists which computers or groups may join.
- **Collector-initiated (pull)**: the WEC is preconfigured with a named list of sources. It suits a small, specific set of machines.

**Client prerequisites (via GPO):** set the subscription manager URI, start the **WinRM** service, and add **Network Service** to the built-in **Event Log Readers** group so the forwarder can read the secured Security channel.

**Collector:** run `wecutil qc` to configure the Windows Event Collector service, then create subscriptions. By default events go to the **ForwardedEvents** log. Delivery options are Normal, Minimize bandwidth, Minimize latency, or Custom (via wecutil). In a domain, traffic is protected by Kerberos.

**Sentinel side:** install AMA on the WEC (Arc if on-premises) and use the **Windows Forwarded Events** connector. Data goes to **WindowsEvent**. Plan capacity at roughly 3,000 events per second per WEC.

terms.d: Windows Event Collector: the server that receives forwarded events into ForwardedEvents.
Clients push events to the collector after GPO configures the subscription manager.
Built-in group; Network Service must be a member so WEF can read the Security log.
Windows Remote Management, the transport WEF uses between source and collector.

lessons.trap: If forwarded events are missing only from the Security channel, the fix is adding Network Service to Event Log Readers, not reinstalling the AMA.
lessons.example: 2,000 workstations use a GPO to forward to one WEC. Only the WEC has AMA and Arc, and its Forwarded Events DCR sends data to the WindowsEvent table.

lessons.title: Syslog via AMA and the log forwarder
lessons.short: Syslog via AMA collects Linux and appliance syslog into the Syslog table. Devices send to a Linux log forwarder running rsyslog or syslog-ng. The AMA on the forwarder applies a DCR that selects facilities and a minimum severity. Non-Azure forwarders need Azure Arc.
lessons.deep:
Many network and security devices can only speak syslog. The pattern is: device → **log forwarder** (a Linux VM) → AMA → workspace.

**Steps:**
1. Install the **Syslog** solution from the Content hub and open **Syslog via AMA**.
2. **+Create data collection rule**: choose the forwarder (an Azure VM or **Arc-enabled** server). The AMA is installed automatically.
3. On **Collect**, choose a **minimum log level per facility**. Choosing a level includes it and every more severe level. For example, LOG_ERR also gives LOG_CRIT, LOG_ALERT and LOG_EMERG.
4. Run `Forwarder_AMA_installer.py` on the forwarder. It configures **rsyslog** or **syslog-ng** to listen for remote messages and opens **port 514 TCP and UDP**.

**Inside the forwarder:** the daemon receives on 514 and hands messages to the AMA (TCP **28330** on AMA 1.28.11+). The AMA sends them to the **Syslog** table. Prerequisites are Python 2.7 or 3, a supported Linux distro, and enough disk. Configure the daemon not to store unneeded logs locally, or a full disk can stop the AMA.

For scale, put several forwarders (or a VM scale set) behind a load balancer. For finer level filtering than 'minimum level', create the DCR through the API.

terms.d: Linux VM that receives syslog from devices and passes it to the AMA.
Syslog category (auth, authpriv, daemon, local0–7…) used to pick what to collect.
Syslog priority from LOG_DEBUG to LOG_EMERG; DCR picks a minimum.
Workspace table for plain syslog messages (Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage…).

lessons.trap: Exam answers sometimes say devices should send to their own local daemon. They must send to the forwarder's daemon, and the forwarder needs Arc if it isn't in Azure.
lessons.example: A Linux web farm sends auth and authpriv at LOG_WARNING and above to two Arc-enabled forwarders. Their DCR lands the messages in Syslog.

lessons.title: CEF via AMA and duplicate avoidance
lessons.short: CEF via AMA collects Common Event Format messages from firewalls and security appliances into CommonSecurityLog, using the same forwarder design as Syslog via AMA. If CEF and Syslog DCRs share a facility, events duplicate across both tables. Separate the facilities, or drop CEF from the Syslog stream with a DCR transformation.
lessons.deep:
**Common Event Format (CEF)** is a syslog-based format built for SIEMs. Its header carries vendor, product, version, event class ID, name and severity, followed by key=value extensions (src, dst, suser, act…). Sentinel parses it into **CommonSecurityLog** columns such as DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP and Activity.

**Configuration** mirrors Syslog via AMA. Install the **Common Event Format** solution, open **CEF via AMA**, create a DCR targeting the forwarder, pick facilities and a minimum severity, then run the same **Forwarder_AMA_installer.py** (port 514). Finally, configure the appliance to send CEF to the forwarder's IP. A test can be sent with `logger` or netcat. Data may take about 20 minutes to appear.

**Duplicate ingestion:** if the same facility is collected by both a CEF DCR and a Syslog DCR on one forwarder, every CEF event lands in both CommonSecurityLog and Syslog (paying twice). Fixes:
1. Send CEF devices on facilities the Syslog DCR does not collect (e.g. local4 for CEF only).
2. If you can't change the device, add an ingestion-time **transformation** to the Syslog DCR that drops CEF, e.g. `source | where ProcessName !contains "CEF" and SyslogMessage !contains "CEF:0"`.

terms.d: Common Event Format: syslog-carried, vendor-neutral format with header plus key=value extensions.
Workspace table that stores parsed CEF (and Cisco ASA) events.
KQL in a DCR (transformKql) that filters or reshapes records before storage.

lessons.trap: CEF events do not go to the Syslog table by design. Seeing them in both tables means a facility overlap, not a connector bug.
lessons.example: A Fortinet firewall sends CEF on local7, and the Linux hosts' Syslog DCR also collects local7. Moving the firewall to local4 stops the double-billing.

lessons.title: Azure Activity logs via Azure Policy
lessons.short: The Azure Activity connector streams subscription-level control-plane events (ARM operations, service health) into the AzureActivity table. You connect it with the Launch Azure Policy Assignment wizard: pick the subscription scope and the workspace, and create a remediation task so existing subscriptions get the diagnostic setting.
lessons.deep:
The **Azure Activity log** records *who did what* on Azure resources: create, update and delete through **Azure Resource Manager**, plus role assignments, policy events and service health. It's the first place to look for attacker persistence in Azure, such as new role assignments or disabled diagnostics.

**Current method (policy-based diagnostic settings):**
1. Install the **Azure Activity** solution from the Content hub.
2. On the connector page choose **Launch Azure Policy Assignment wizard**.
3. **Basics**: set the **scope** (a subscription, or a management group to cover many).
4. **Parameters**: choose the primary **Log Analytics workspace** (the Sentinel workspace).
5. **Remediation**: tick **Create a remediation task**. Policy only acts automatically on new or updated resources, so the task fixes existing ones. The assignment uses a managed identity to deploy the setting.
6. Review + create.

You need the **Owner** role on the assignment scope. Data lands in **AzureActivity**. If an older legacy connection exists, use **Disconnect All** on the connector page before switching.

terms.d: Subscription-level log of ARM control-plane operations and service events.
Azure Policy job that applies a deployIfNotExists policy to already-existing non-compliant resources.
Workspace table holding the activity log events.

lessons.trap: Without a remediation task, existing subscriptions are not connected. Policy only applies automatically to new or changed resources.
lessons.example: A tenant with 40 subscriptions assigns the activity-log policy at the root management group and creates a remediation task. All 40 start streaming to AzureActivity.

lessons.title: Resource diagnostic settings
lessons.short: Azure resource logs (Key Vault, Storage, NSG flow, SQL…) reach Sentinel through diagnostic settings. Standalone connectors have you add a diagnostic setting on each resource with 'Send to Log Analytics workspace'. Policy-managed connectors apply one setting to every resource of that type in a scope, and need Owner on that scope.
lessons.deep:
Every Azure resource can export **resource logs** and metrics through a **diagnostic setting**. A setting names the log categories and the destination: a Log Analytics workspace, storage account, event hub or partner solution.

**Standalone (per resource):** connector page → open the resource → **Diagnostic settings** → **+ Add diagnostic setting**. Name it, tick the log categories (and metrics if needed), choose **Send to Log Analytics workspace**, then select the Sentinel workspace and **Save**. This works well for a handful of resources.

**Managed by Azure Policy (at scale):** the connector's **Launch Azure Policy Assignment wizard** assigns a built-in deployIfNotExists policy for that resource type. You set the scope (subscription or resource group), the workspace, and which log types are True. A **remediation task** covers existing resources. New resources are configured automatically. You need **Owner** on the policy assignment scope.

**Gotchas:**
- A policy-managed connector shows *connected* only if data arrived in the last **14 days**.
- Storage accounts need settings on the child services (blob, file, queue, table) to get their logs.
- A diagnostic setting writes to resource-specific or AzureDiagnostics tables depending on the service and the mode you choose.

terms.d: Per-resource export of chosen log categories and metrics to a destination.
Azure Policy effect that deploys a configuration (here, a diagnostic setting) when it's missing.
Data-plane logs emitted by an Azure resource, e.g. Key Vault AuditEvent.

lessons.trap: Adding a diagnostic setting to one Key Vault doesn't cover Key Vaults created next month. Azure Policy does.
lessons.example: Security requires logs from every Key Vault, including future ones. The analyst uses the Key Vault connector's policy wizard at subscription scope and creates a remediation task.

lessons.title: Ingesting threat indicators
lessons.short: Threat intelligence reaches Sentinel as STIX objects. The sources are the Threat Intelligence – TAXII connector (TAXII 2.0/2.1 servers), the Threat Intelligence Upload API (for TIPs and custom apps), Microsoft's own Defender Threat Intelligence connector, bulk file import (CSV or STIX JSON), and manual creation. Indicators are stored in ThreatIntelIndicators and ThreatIntelObjects.
lessons.deep:
**STIX** describes threat intelligence (indicators, threat actors, attack patterns, identities, relationships). **TAXII** is the protocol that serves STIX collections.

**Ingestion options:**
- **Threat Intelligence – TAXII**: built-in TAXII client for **TAXII 2.0 or 2.1** servers. You supply a friendly name, the **API root URL**, the **collection ID**, credentials if needed, and a polling frequency. Repeat for each collection.
- **Threat Intelligence Upload API**: REST endpoint for threat intelligence platforms (TIPs) and custom apps. It takes STIX format at workspace scope, needs no data connector, and its Entra app needs **Microsoft Sentinel Contributor**. It replaces the deprecated **TIP connector**, which used the Graph `tiIndicators` API.
- **Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence connector**: Microsoft-curated indicators.
- **Import from file**: CSV (indicators only, up to 50 MB) or STIX 2.1 JSON (up to 250 MB), through Threat intelligence > Import > Import using a file.
- **Manual**: add objects in the threat intelligence management page.

**Storage:** STIX indicators go to **ThreatIntelIndicators**, other STIX objects to **ThreatIntelObjects**. The legacy **ThreatIntelligenceIndicator** table stopped receiving data after July 2025. Sentinel re-ingests intel every 7–10 days.

terms.d: Structured Threat Information Expression: standard JSON model for threat intelligence objects.
Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information: HTTPS protocol that serves STIX collections.
Sentinel REST API that accepts STIX objects from TIPs or scripts without a connector.
Current workspace table storing STIX indicator objects.

lessons.trap: Writing new hunting queries against ThreatIntelligenceIndicator is outdated. The current tables are ThreatIntelIndicators and ThreatIntelObjects.
lessons.example: An ISAC publishes a TAXII 2.1 feed. The SOC adds a TAXII connector with the ISAC's API root and collection ID, and indicators appear on the Threat intelligence page within minutes.

lessons.title: Custom log tables
lessons.short: Data with no built-in table goes into a custom table ending in _CL. DCR-based custom tables are created from the workspace Tables page (or API, CLI, ARM) with a sample JSON file, a DCR, an optional transformation, and a plan (Analytics, Basic or Auxiliary). Data arrives via the Logs Ingestion API or Custom Logs via AMA.
lessons.deep:
**Creating the table:** Log Analytics workspace → **Tables** → **Create** → new custom log (DCR-based). Then:
- **Name**: the portal adds the `_CL` suffix automatically. In API, CLI, PowerShell, ARM or Bicep you must add it yourself.
- **Plan**: **Analytics** (default, full KQL and alerting), **Basic**, or **Auxiliary/data lake** (cheap, limited querying). Choose by how the data will be used.
- **DCR** (new or existing) and, if needed, a **data collection endpoint (DCE)**.
- **Sample JSON** with at least one record. The portal infers the schema from it.
- **Transformation editor**: KQL run on every incoming record, e.g. `source | extend TimeGenerated = todatetime(Time)`.

Every table needs **TimeGenerated**. If the sample lacks it, the transformation adds it. Custom columns added to built-in Azure tables end in `_CF`. Managing tables needs `Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/*`, which **Log Analytics Contributor** includes.

**Feeding it:**
- **Logs Ingestion API**: app registration + secret, the **Monitoring Metrics Publisher** role on the DCR, POST to the DCR's stream (`Custom-<table>`). It replaces the legacy HTTP Data Collector API.
- **Custom Logs via AMA**: text files on servers. Create the `_CL` table first with **TimeGenerated** and **RawData**, then a DCR with a file pattern (wildcards allowed).

terms.d: Mandatory suffix for custom log tables in a Log Analytics workspace.
Analytics, Basic or Auxiliary: sets cost, query capability and retention behaviour.
Role an app needs on the DCR to send data via the Logs Ingestion API.
Data collection endpoint; needed for Private Link or DCRs without a built-in ingestion endpoint.

lessons.trap: Granting the app Log Analytics Contributor on the workspace won't let it send data. It needs Monitoring Metrics Publisher on the DCR.
lessons.example: A badge-access system exports JSON. The engineer creates BadgeAccess_CL with a sample file, a transformation that maps the event time to TimeGenerated, and a DCR, then sends data through the Logs Ingestion API.

lessons.title: Custom detections from Advanced Hunting
lessons.short: A custom detection rule is a saved Advanced Hunting KQL query that runs on a schedule and raises alerts. Results must include Timestamp (or TimeGenerated) plus the event's ReportId, with DeviceId for Defender for Endpoint tables. Frequencies are Continuous (NRT), every 1, 3, 12 or 24 hours, or Custom for Sentinel data.
lessons.deep:
In the Defender portal, write a query in **Advanced hunting** and choose **Create detection rule** (or go to Hunting > Custom detection rules > + Create). Microsoft now recommends custom detections for new rules across Defender XDR and Sentinel data.

**Required output columns:**
- **Timestamp** or **TimeGenerated**: sets the alert time.
- **ReportId**: identifies the source event. With **DeviceId** it's needed for Defender for Endpoint (Device*) tables. Other Defender tables need Timestamp and ReportId from the same event.
- Entity columns for mapping, e.g. DeviceId/DeviceName, AccountObjectId/AccountSid/AccountUpn, RecipientEmailAddress.
When summarising, keep them with `arg_max(Timestamp, ReportId)`.

**Frequency → Defender data lookback:** every 24 h → 30 days; 12 h → 48 h; 3 h → 12 h; 1 h → 4 h. **Continuous (NRT)** runs in near real time but the query must use one table, no joins, unions or externaldata, and no comment lines. **Custom** frequency (5 minutes–14 days) applies to Sentinel data only.

On save, the rule immediately checks the past 30 days. Each run creates **at most 150 alerts**. Don't filter on Timestamp yourself, because the service applies the lookback.

To create rules on Defender XDR data you need **Security settings (manage)**, or an Entra role such as Security Administrator. Rules over Sentinel data need **Microsoft Sentinel Contributor**.

terms.d: Scheduled Advanced Hunting query in Defender XDR that generates alerts and optional actions.
Event identifier column that a custom detection needs to link alerts to source records.
Near-real-time custom detection option with single-table, no-join query limits.
KQL aggregation that returns the row with the max value, used to keep Timestamp and ReportId.

lessons.trap: A query that summarises by DeviceId without Timestamp and ReportId can't be saved as a detection. Keep them with arg_max.
lessons.example: A hunter finds certutil downloading files. They project Timestamp, DeviceId, ReportId and AccountUpn, then save the query as an hourly custom detection scoped to server device groups.

lessons.title: Custom detection alert details and actions
lessons.short: The rule wizard sets the alert's details: unique name and title, severity, category, MITRE techniques, description and recommended actions. It also sets impacted entities and optional automatic response actions on devices, files, users or email. Dynamic {{Column}} placeholders and up to 20 custom details enrich each alert.
lessons.deep:
**Alert details:** detection name and alert title (both unique), **severity**, **category**, MITRE ATT&CK **techniques**, description and recommended actions. A threat analytics report can be linked. Titles and descriptions can include up to three `{{ColumnName}}` dynamic values, e.g. `{{AccountName}} signed in from {{Country}}`. **Custom details** (up to 20 key-value pairs, 4 KB per alert) surface query fields on the alert.

**Impacted entities:** pick one column per entity type (device, user, mailbox). Defender entities map automatically, while Sentinel data must be mapped manually.

**Actions (Defender data only):**
- **Devices** (needs DeviceId): isolate device, collect investigation package, run antivirus scan, initiate investigation, restrict app execution.
- **Files**: allow/block (adds an indicator, can be scoped to device groups), quarantine file (needs a SHA1 or SHA256 column).
- **Users**: mark as compromised (sets the Entra ID user risk to high), disable user, reset user authentication. Disable and reset need a SID column such as AccountSid.
- **Email**: move to a mailbox folder (Junk, Inbox, Deleted items) or soft/hard delete. Needs NetworkMessageId and RecipientEmailAddress.

**Scope:** all devices or chosen device groups. This only affects device-based rules. You must have access to every device in scope.

terms.d: {{Column}} placeholders that insert query values into alert titles and descriptions.
Up to 20 key-value fields from query results attached to each alert.
Action that raises the user's Entra ID Protection risk level to high.

lessons.trap: Email actions fail silently if NetworkMessageId or RecipientEmailAddress is missing. Each action needs its own identifier columns.
lessons.example: A rule spotting malicious macro attachments outputs NetworkMessageId and RecipientEmailAddress, so it can soft-delete the message from every recipient's mailbox automatically.

lessons.title: Managing custom detection rules
lessons.short: Custom detections are managed at Hunting > Custom detection rules in the Defender portal. The list shows Last run, Last run status, Next run and Status. From a rule you can Run it now, Edit it, Modify query in Advanced Hunting, Turn off/on, or Delete it, and you can review its Triggered alerts and Triggered actions.
lessons.deep:
**Where:** Defender portal → **Hunting** → **Custom detection rules**. When a Sentinel workspace is onboarded to the Defender portal, Sentinel analytics rules are listed here too. You can search by name or ID and filter on any column, including workspace.

**Columns:**
- **Last run**: when the rule last checked for matches.
- **Last run status**: did it succeed (custom detections only).
- **Next run**: when it runs next.
- **Status**: on or off.

**Actions on a rule:**
- **Run**: runs immediately and resets the interval for the next run.
- **Edit**: reopens the wizard (details, entities, actions, scope).
- **Modify query**: opens the query in Advanced Hunting.
- **Turn off / Turn on**: pause without losing the rule.
- **Delete**: turns it off and removes it permanently.
- **Include/exclude from correlation**: Sentinel analytics rules only.

**Rule details page:** general info and run status, **Triggered alerts** (set status and classification, link to an incident, rerun the query) and **Triggered actions** (what automatic responses ran).

**Housekeeping:** check Last run status after table or schema changes, turn off noisy rules while tuning, and use the least-privileged role (Security settings manage) rather than Global Administrator.

terms.d: Indicates whether a custom detection's latest execution succeeded.
Tab listing automatic response actions a rule performed.
Immediate execution that also resets the rule's next scheduled run.

lessons.trap: To stop a noisy rule while keeping it for later, choose Turn off, not Delete. Delete is permanent.
lessons.example: A rule's Last run status shows failures after a column was renamed. The analyst uses Modify query, fixes the column, saves, then selects Run to confirm.

lessons.title: Scheduled analytics rules
lessons.short: A scheduled analytics rule runs KQL on a fixed interval over a lookback window (both 5 minutes–14 days) and raises an alert when results cross a threshold. The wizard covers the query, entity mapping, custom details, alert details, scheduling, event grouping, suppression, incident settings and alert grouping, plus automated response.
lessons.deep:
**General:** name, description, **severity** (Informational/Low/Medium/High), and MITRE tactics and techniques. Many rules start from a **rule template** that comes with a Content hub solution.

**Set rule logic:**
- **Query**: 1–10,000 characters, no `search *` or `union *`. Prefer ASIM parsers.
- **Entity mapping**: up to **10** mappings, each with up to 3 identifiers, and up to 500 entities per alert in total.
- **Custom details** and **alert details** (dynamic name and description) go into ExtendedProperties.
- **Run query every** ≤ **Lookup data from the last**. Each can be 5 min–14 days. Rules run with a built-in 5-minute delay to allow for ingestion.
- **Alert threshold**: more than, less than or equal to N results.
- **Event grouping**: one alert summarising all results (default), or one alert per result (up to 150 per run).
- **Suppression**: stop running for up to 24 hours after an alert.

**Incident settings:** create incidents (on by default). **Alert grouping** puts related alerts into one incident within a window (default 5 hours, up to 7 days). It can group when all entities match, group all alerts from the rule, or match selected entities and details. In the Defender portal, the Defender XDR correlation engine makes the final grouping decisions, and closed incidents aren't reopened.

**Automated response:** attach automation rules.

terms.d: 'Lookup data from the last' window each run queries.
Choice between one alert per run or one alert per query result.
Incident setting that groups related alerts into one incident within a time window.
Stops the rule from running for a set time after it fires (max 24 h).

lessons.trap: Run interval longer than lookback creates coverage gaps and fails validation. The interval must be less than or equal to the lookback.
lessons.example: A brute-force rule runs every 10 minutes over 10 minutes of SigninLogs, triggers when more than 0 results return, and groups alerts by matching account into one incident per 5 hours.

lessons.title: Near-real-time (NRT) rules
lessons.short: NRT rules are a fast subset of scheduled rules that run every minute over data ingested in the previous minute. They query on ingestion time, so ingestion latency doesn't cause misses. There are limits: 50 NRT rules per customer, up to 30 single-event alerts per run, and only sources with ingestion delay under 12 hours.
lessons.deep:
Create an NRT rule from Analytics → **Create → NRT query rule**, or from an NRT template. The wizard looks like the scheduled wizard, but without interval and lookback, because those are fixed.

**Behaviour:**
- Runs **once a minute** with a 2-minute built-in delay (scheduled rules use 5).
- Queries on **ingestion time**, not TimeGenerated, so late-arriving events are still evaluated once.
- Supports entity mapping, custom details, dynamic alert details, incident and alert grouping, suppression, and automation rules.
- Can query several tables and workspaces.

**Limits:**
- **50 NRT rules per customer**.
- Each run produces up to **30 single-event alerts**. With more matches, 29 alerts are created plus a 30th summary alert.
- Event grouping is limited.
- Works properly only on sources with an ingestion delay **under 12 hours**, and gives no real benefit on high-latency sources.

**When to choose NRT:** high-value, low-volume signals where every minute counts, such as a break-glass account sign-in, a security log cleared (1102), or a disabled diagnostic setting. For aggregation over long windows (hours or days of history), use a scheduled rule.

terms.d: Sentinel analytics rule fixed to a one-minute cadence over freshly ingested data.
When a record reached the workspace; NRT rules evaluate on this rather than TimeGenerated.
One alert per matching event, the NRT output model (max 30 per run).

lessons.trap: Choosing NRT to count failed logons over 24 hours is wrong. NRT only sees the last minute of ingested data.
lessons.example: The SOC wants an alert within about two minutes of any sign-in by a break-glass account. An NRT rule on SigninLogs filtered to that UPN fits.

lessons.title: Threat intelligence and ML analytics rules
lessons.short: Besides scheduled and NRT rules, Sentinel offers built-in rule types you enable but can't customise. Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence Analytics matches Microsoft indicators against CEF, DNS and Syslog data. ML behavior analytics flags anomalous SSH and RDP logins. Fusion correlates multistage attacks but is disabled when Sentinel is onboarded to the Defender portal.
lessons.deep:
**Threat intelligence rules:**
- **Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence Analytics** (TI matching): enable it from **Rule templates**.
