It matches Microsoft's domain, IP and URL indicators against CommonSecurityLog, DnsEvents, Syslog and others, producing high-fidelity alerts. Its logic is read-only. Severity depends on the match, e.g. allowed traffic to a bad IP is High, blocked is lower.
- **TI map templates** (scheduled rules such as 'TI map IP entity to SigninLogs') join your ingested indicators (ThreatIntelIndicators) against log tables. You *can* edit these because they're ordinary scheduled rules.

**Machine learning rules:**
- **ML behavior analytics**: built-in, non-customisable detections of anomalous **SSH** (Linux) and **RDP** (Windows) logins.
- **Anomaly** rules: ML baselines that write to the Anomalies table (covered in the anomalies lesson).
- **Fusion**: an ML correlation engine that turns many low-fidelity signals into multistage-attack incidents. It is on by default and there is only one Fusion rule.

**Defender portal effect:** when Sentinel is onboarded to the Defender portal (or Defender XDR incident integration is on), **Fusion** and **Microsoft Security incident creation rules** are disabled. Defender XDR's correlation engine takes over incident creation. Microsoft recommends custom detections for new rules.

terms.d: Built-in, non-editable rule matching Microsoft TI against your CEF, DNS and Syslog logs.
Scheduled-rule templates joining ingested indicators to log tables; editable.
Built-in ML rules detecting anomalous SSH and RDP logins.
ML correlation engine for multistage attacks; replaced by XDR correlation in the Defender portal.

lessons.trap: 'Edit the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Analytics query' is not possible. To customise TI matching, use or clone a TI map scheduled rule.
lessons.example: A SOC ingests a partner TAXII feed and wants alerts when Entra sign-ins come from those IPs. They enable the TI map IP entity to SigninLogs template.

lessons.title: MITRE ATT&CK coverage
lessons.short: The MITRE ATT&CK page in Sentinel (Threat management > MITRE ATT&CK) maps your active scheduled and NRT analytics rules onto ATT&CK tactics and techniques. Simulated coverage shows what available templates would add. Rules, hunting queries and bookmarks carry technique tags, and incidents inherit them from their alerts.
lessons.deep:
**MITRE ATT&CK** is a public knowledge base of adversary **tactics** (the 'why', e.g. Initial Access, Persistence, Lateral Movement) and **techniques/sub-techniques** (the 'how', e.g. T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter).

**In Sentinel** (Defender portal: Microsoft Sentinel > Threat management > **MITRE ATT&CK**, currently preview):
- The matrix shows **active coverage**: by default, enabled **scheduled** and **NRT** rules counted per technique, with a legend showing density.
- **Simulated** coverage: pick items from the Simulated rules menu (such as available rule templates) to see how coverage would change if you enabled them. This is a gap-analysis tool.
- Select a technique to open the details pane, which links to the MITRE page and to related active detections and hunting queries.
- Search by technique name or ID, or filter by threat scenario.

**Tagging:** set tactics and techniques in the analytics rule wizard (General tab). Custom detections and hunting queries carry them too, bookmarks can inherit or override them, and incidents gain the techniques of their alerts.

**Workflow for exam scenarios:** open the matrix, find empty techniques that matter to your threat model, simulate templates, enable or author rules, and tag them correctly so the matrix stays accurate.

terms.d: ATT&CK column describing the adversary's goal, e.g. Credential Access.
ATT&CK entry describing how a goal is achieved, with an ID such as T1003.
MITRE page view showing coverage you'd gain by enabling available detections.

lessons.trap: A disabled rule or an untagged rule doesn't count as coverage. The matrix only reflects active rules with techniques set.
lessons.example: Before an audit, the SOC lead sees zero coverage under Exfiltration, simulates rule templates for that tactic, then enables three of them.

lessons.title: Anomalies in Microsoft Sentinel
lessons.short: Anomaly rules are machine-learning templates that baseline behaviour and write unusual activity to the Anomalies table. They don't create alerts or incidents. Built-in anomaly rules can't be edited. You duplicate one to make a single '- Customized' copy, tune its threshold and parameters in Flighting mode, then promote it to Production.
lessons.deep:
**Purpose:** anomalies are lower-fidelity signals. On their own they don't prove an attack, but they add context to hunting and investigations and can strengthen other detections. Some come from the **UEBA** engine, which baselines each entity against its own history, its peers and the organisation.

**Where they show:** the **Anomalies** table (query it in Logs), not in alerts or incidents. Example:
`Anomalies | where RuleId contains "<RuleId>"`, then expand **AnomalyReasons** to see why one fired. Too many anomalies means the threshold is too low.

**Tuning workflow:**
1. Open the anomaly rule (Analytics → Anomalies tab). You can't edit or delete the built-in rule, only switch it between **Production** and **Flighting**.
2. **Duplicate** it. The copy is named '<original> - Customized', starts disabled and in **Flighting** (FLGT badge). Only one customised copy per rule is allowed.
3. Edit the copy's **threshold** and the parameters its algorithm exposes. The results preview shows the effect.
4. Compare the outputs: `Anomalies | where AnomalyTemplateId contains "<RuleId>"`.
5. Switch the copy to **Production**. The original flips to Flighting automatically, because only one version can be in Production.

To change the template version of an active anomaly rule you must recreate it.

terms.d: Workspace table where anomaly rules record unusual behaviour; no alerts are created.
Test mode in which an anomaly rule runs and logs results without being the production version.
The single duplicate of a built-in anomaly rule that you can tune.

lessons.trap: Expecting anomaly rules to raise incidents is the classic mistake. They only write to the Anomalies table.
lessons.example: An 'anomalous sign-in volume' rule is too chatty. The analyst duplicates it, raises the threshold in Flighting, compares a week of output, then promotes the copy to Production.

lessons.title: Investigating and remediating email threats with Defender for Office 365
lessons.short: Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 gives analysts Threat Explorer, automated investigation and response (AIR) and email remediation actions such as soft delete, hard delete and move to junk. Every action is tracked in the Action center.
lessons.deep:
**Hunting tools.** Plan 1 includes **Real-time detections** (malicious mail at delivery time). Plan 2 adds **Threat Explorer**, with extra views (All email, Campaigns, URL clicks), saved queries, post-delivery data and **Go hunt**.

**Remediation actions.** From Threat Explorer (**Take action**), advanced hunting or an AIR investigation you can: **Move to junk**, **Move to inbox**, **Move to deleted items**, **Soft delete** (recoverable from Recoverable Items), **Hard delete** (purged; admins can still use single-item recovery) and **Delete sender's copy**. In Explorer you can pick up to 100 messages by hand or act on a whole query.

**Approvals.** For the action to be approved you need the **Search and Purge** role (or the unified RBAC *Email & collaboration advanced actions (manage)* permission). With **two-step approval**, one analyst adds messages to a remediation and another approves it from the Action center **Pending** tab. The **History** tab shows the last 30 days.

**AIR.** Alerts such as user-reported phish, ZAP, URL clicks and compromised-user detections start automated investigations. By default their recommended actions wait for approval. Admins can opt specific clusters into **automated remediation** (*Settings > Email & collaboration > MDO automation settings*); the only action it uses is **soft delete**.

**Compromised mailbox.** Disable the account or reset its password, revoke sessions, check MFA methods and consented apps, remove forwarding and hidden inbox rules, then unblock the user from **Restricted entities** if it was stopped for sending spam.

terms.d: Plan 2 hunting tool for email, covering delivery and post-delivery events, with remediation actions.
Moves mail to Recoverable Items\Deletions; users and admins can still recover it.
Automated investigation and response: playbooks that investigate alerts and recommend remediation.
Defender portal page that lists users blocked from sending mail, for example after outbound spam.

lessons.trap: Exams contrast Real-time detections (Plan 1) with Threat Explorer (Plan 2), and soft delete (recoverable) with hard delete (purged).
lessons.example: A phishing message reached 300 inboxes. The analyst queries it in Threat Explorer, chooses Take action > Soft delete, and a second analyst approves the remediation in the Action center.

lessons.title: Automatic attack disruption across Defender XDR
lessons.short: Automatic attack disruption uses high-confidence, correlated XDR signals to contain an attack while it is still running. It can disable or contain users, contain devices or IPs, and revoke sessions. Affected incidents get an Attack Disruption tag.
lessons.deep:
**What it is.** When Defender XDR correlates signals into a high-confidence incident, such as ransomware, business email compromise (BEC) or adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing, it acts automatically to cut the attacker off.

**Actions.** **Contain device**, **Contain IP** and **Contain user** (Defender for Endpoint), **Disable user** (Defender for Identity in AD, or through a Microsoft-managed app in Entra ID), and **Revoke user session** / suspend in Microsoft Entra ID. It can also handle OAuth app compromise through Defender for Cloud Apps. Microsoft Sentinel connectors add preview actions for Okta and AWS.

**Prerequisites.** You need a qualifying licence (such as Microsoft 365 E5) and the relevant workloads deployed. For Defender for Endpoint, set device-group automation to **Full** (recommended), use **Standard discovery**, and keep the sensor current. Defender for Identity needs a sensor on the domain controller that holds the account. Defender for Office 365 needs Exchange Online mailboxes with audit actions such as MailItemsAccessed, UpdateInboxRules, MoveToDeletedItems, SoftDelete and HardDelete. Defender Antivirus mode doesn't matter.

**Seeing it.** The incident shows an **Attack Disruption** tag, a yellow banner and contained assets in the graph, and the action is logged in the **Action center**. You can query it in the `DisruptionAndResponseEvents` table.

**Control.** Add exclusions under *Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Automated response* (users, device groups, IPs). After investigating, release a contained device or select **Enable user**. Opting out completely requires a support case.

terms.d: Label on incidents in which automatic disruption took action.
Defender for Endpoint policy that blocks a compromised account's activity on onboarded devices.
Users, device groups or IPs that are kept out of automatic containment.

lessons.trap: Releasing a contained asset is a manual step (release from containment or Enable user). Exclusions are preventive, so they don't undo an action that has already run.
lessons.example: An AiTM phishing attack steals a session cookie. Defender XDR disables the user and revokes the user's sessions within minutes, and the incident appears with the Attack Disruption tag.

lessons.title: Microsoft Purview DLP alerts in the Defender portal
lessons.short: Microsoft Purview data loss prevention (DLP) alerts flow into the Defender XDR incident queue, where analysts correlate them with other alerts and remediate files, emails, users and devices without leaving the portal.
lessons.deep:
**Licensing and flow.** With E5/A5 (or E5 Compliance / Information Protection & Governance), DLP alerts flow to Defender automatically. In the Purview portal you must **turn on alerts for your DLP policies**. Administrative unit restrictions carry over, so a scoped admin sees only alerts for that unit.

**Investigating.** Filter the queue by service/detection source **Microsoft Data Loss Prevention**. A DLP alert page shows the **alert story** (matched policy and sensitive information types), **Related events**, a **Sensitive info types** tab and a **Source** tab with the matched content. Viewing the source requires specific permissions, and downloading the file needs the **Data classification content viewer** role.

**Hunting.** DLP audit data is in the **CloudAppEvents** table, about 30 days of activity, which requires the Microsoft 365 connector in Defender for Cloud Apps.

**Remediation.** For SharePoint or OneDrive files you can **apply a retention label**, **apply a sensitivity label**, **unshare**, **delete** or **download**. For email you can download the message. Use the user and device cards for identity and endpoint actions, and **Manage incident** to assign, tag or resolve.

**Roles.** Manage Alerts gives access to DLP and security alerts. Information Protection Analyst and DLP Compliance Management give access to DLP alerts only.

terms.d: Alert raised when content matches a Purview DLP policy rule.
Purview role needed to see or download the content that matched.
Advanced hunting table that holds Microsoft 365 app activity, including DLP audit data.

lessons.trap: If DLP alerts are missing from Defender, the fix is usually in Purview (alerts not turned on for the policy). Adding a Sentinel connector doesn't fix it.
lessons.example: A DLP alert shows a spreadsheet of credit card numbers shared externally from OneDrive. The analyst unshares the file and applies a Highly Confidential sensitivity label from the alert page.

lessons.title: Insider risk management alerts in Defender XDR
lessons.short: Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management (IRM) alerts can appear in the Defender XDR alert and incident queue and in advanced hunting. Only users who hold an IRM role can see that data.
lessons.deep:
**Why it matters.** A user downloads thousands of files just before resigning. On its own, that is an insider risk signal. Combined with a Defender for Endpoint USB alert or a Defender for Cloud Apps mass-download alert, it becomes a stronger, correlated incident.

**Integration.** IRM alerts, indicators and events appear in the unified **alert and incident queue**. They are also available in **advanced hunting** (tables such as `DataSecurityBehaviors` and `DataSecurityEvents`), the Microsoft Graph security API and Microsoft Sentinel through the Defender XDR connector.

**Setup.** In IRM settings, an admin turns on data sharing with other security solutions.

**Privacy controls.** Inside the IRM solution, usernames can be pseudonymized. In Defender XDR, IRM data isn't pseudonymized, so it can be correlated with endpoint and cloud-app alerts. To compensate, access is restricted: only users with **Insider Risk Management analyst or investigator roles** in Purview can view IRM data in Defender.

**Response.** Analysts correlate the IRM alert with other evidence in the incident, then escalate inside Purview, for example by opening an IRM case, or act on the identity or device.

terms.d: Purview solution that detects risky user activity such as data theft by departing employees.
Masking usernames in IRM views. It doesn't apply to IRM data shown in Defender XDR.
Advanced hunting table with IRM and data security events.

lessons.trap: A Security Administrator in Defender doesn't automatically see IRM alerts. They need an IRM analyst or investigator role in Purview.
lessons.example: The SOC sees an incident that combines an IRM 'data theft by departing user' alert with a Defender for Endpoint removable storage alert on the same laptop.

lessons.title: Defender for Cloud workload protection alerts
lessons.short: Defender for Cloud workload protection plans (Servers, Storage, Containers, Databases and others) raise security alerts that appear in the Defender XDR queue. Analysts respond with the Take action tab, Logic App workflow automation and suppression rules.
lessons.deep:
**Alerts.** Each enabled plan generates alerts with a severity: **High** (high confidence the activity is malicious, for example Mimikatz), **Medium** (suspicious, often anomaly-based), **Low** (possibly benign or blocked, for example log clearing) and **Informational**. Alerts stay visible for 90 days.

**Defender XDR integration.** Defender for Cloud alerts and incidents are correlated in the Defender portal, and cloud resources appear in the attack story. **Informational alerts are not sent.** Status changes to Defender for Cloud alerts sync in both directions. Defender for Endpoint alerts on cloud VMs show in both products, but their status doesn't sync. Filter the queue by **alert subscription ID**. Sentinel customers should use the **tenant-based** Defender for Cloud connector and disconnect the subscription-based legacy one to avoid duplicates.

**Take action tab.**
- **Inspect resource context**: activity logs for the resource
- **Mitigate the threat**: manual remediation steps
- **Prevent future attacks**: hardening recommendations
- **Trigger automated response**: run a Logic App
- **Suppress similar alerts**: create a suppression rule

**Automation.** Workflow automation runs consumption Logic Apps when an alert, recommendation or compliance change occurs. It needs Security Admin or Owner on the resource group plus **Logic App Contributor** to create the app. **Suppression rules** auto-dismiss matching alerts, with an optional expiry. Security admin or Owner can create them.

terms.d: Defender for Cloud plans that detect threats on servers, storage, containers, databases and other resources.
Rule that automatically sets matching alerts to Dismissed.
Runs a Logic App when a Defender for Cloud alert or recommendation fires.

lessons.trap: For known benign recurring alerts the answer is a suppression rule. Disabling the plan or dismissing alerts by hand is wrong.
lessons.example: Defender for Storage flags malware uploaded to a blob container. The analyst follows the Mitigate the threat steps, applies the hardening recommendations and triggers a Logic App that opens a ticket.

lessons.title: Defender for Cloud Apps risks and governance actions
lessons.short: Defender for Cloud Apps detects anomalies in SaaS apps, such as impossible travel, suspicious inbox forwarding, ransomware activity and risky OAuth apps. Analysts remediate with governance actions like Suspend user, Require user to sign in again and Confirm user compromised.
lessons.deep:
**Detections.** Anomaly detections learn normal behaviour, mostly over about **7 days**. Examples include **Impossible travel**, **Activity from infrequent country**, **Suspicious inbox manipulation rule**, **Suspicious inbox forwarding**, **Unusual file download (by user)**, **Ransomware activity**, **Multiple failed login attempts** and OAuth alerts such as **Unusual ISP for an OAuth app**.

**Classify.** **True positive** (malicious), **Benign true positive** (real but allowed, such as a pen test) or **False positive** (not malicious). An impossible travel alert caused by a corporate VPN is a false positive: dismiss it and tag the VPN IP range so it doesn't recur.

**User governance actions.**
- **Notify user**: sends an email
- **Suspend user**: blocks sign-in, including users already signed in
- **Require user to sign in again**: revokes refresh tokens and session cookies
- **Confirm user compromised**: sets the user's risk to **high** in Microsoft Entra ID Protection, so risk-based policies apply

**App actions.** Revoke an app, ban an app, or revoke all OAuth tokens for a compromised app. **File actions** include remove external users, make private, quarantine and apply a sensitivity label.

**Tracking.** Manual and policy-driven actions are logged in **Cloud Apps > Governance log**, where some can be retried or reverted.

terms.d: Remediation that Defender for Cloud Apps applies to a user, file or app.
Raises user risk to high in Entra ID Protection.
Real activity that is suspicious but authorized, such as a security test.

lessons.trap: Learn the three user actions apart: Suspend blocks sign-in, Require sign in again only revokes sessions, and Confirm compromised changes risk in Entra ID.
lessons.example: A Suspicious inbox forwarding alert shows a finance user's mail auto-forwarded to Gmail. The analyst suspends the user, resets the password and deletes the rule.

lessons.title: Compromised identities in Microsoft Entra ID Protection
lessons.short: Microsoft Entra ID Protection calculates sign-in risk and user risk from detections such as leaked credentials, anonymous IP address and anomalous token. Analysts investigate the risk reports, then remediate through self-service flows or admin actions such as resetting the password or confirming compromise.
lessons.deep:
**Licence.** Full ID Protection requires **Microsoft Entra ID P2** (or Entra Suite).

**Detections.** *Sign-in risk* examples are **Anonymous IP address**, **Atypical travel**, **Unfamiliar sign-in properties**, **Password spray** and **Anomalous token**. *User risk* examples are **Leaked credentials** (offline, always high), **Attacker in the Middle** (always high) and **Microsoft Entra threat intelligence**. Detections are either real-time or offline.

**Self-remediation** (requires risk-based Conditional Access policies). Sign-in risk is remediated when the user completes **MFA**. User risk is remediated by **MFA followed by a secure password change**. Hybrid users who change their password on-premises need **password hash sync** and the **Allow on-premises password change to reset user risk** setting.

**Admin actions.** **Reset password** (temporary password), **Require password change**, **Dismiss risk** (the password doesn't change), **Confirm compromised** and **Confirm safe**. After confirming compromise you can also block the user, revoke refresh tokens (`Revoke-MgUserSignInSession`) and disable devices.

**Least-privilege roles.** **Security Operator** to dismiss risk, **User Administrator** to reset passwords and **Security Administrator** to edit risk policies. In Log Analytics or Sentinel, detections are in `AADUserRiskEvents` and user risk state is in `AADRiskyUsers`.

terms.d: Probability that an identity is compromised, built from user risk detections.
Probability that a specific sign-in wasn't made by the account owner.
Password change after MFA; it clears user risk.
Admin marks risk as handled without changing the password.

lessons.trap: Dismissing risk doesn't reset the password, and user risk self-remediation needs MFA plus a password change, not MFA alone.
lessons.example: Leaked credentials raises a user to high risk. The risk-based policy forces MFA and a secure password change at next sign-in, and the user's state changes to Remediated.

lessons.title: Defender for Identity alerts and response actions
lessons.short: Defender for Identity sensors on domain controllers detect on-premises Active Directory attacks such as reconnaissance, DCSync, Golden Ticket and pass-the-hash. Analysts respond with identity actions like Disable, Revoke session, Mark as compromised and Force password change.
lessons.deep:
**Alert categories.**
- **Reconnaissance and discovery**: account enumeration (LDAP), network-mapping (DNS), SAMR reconnaissance, honeytoken queried via LDAP
- **Persistence and privilege escalation**: Golden Ticket variants, suspicious additions to sensitive groups, AdminSdHolder changes
- **Credential access**: **Suspected DCSync attack**, brute force (Kerberos, NTLM), AS-REP roasting, **Honeytoken authentication activity**
- **Lateral movement**: **pass-the-hash**, **pass-the-ticket**, **overpass-the-hash**, remote code execution over DNS

Defender for Identity alerts can trigger Defender **automated investigation and response**. Classify alerts as **true positive**, **benign true positive** or **false positive**. Classic-format detections are tuned under *Settings > Identities > Excluded entities*. Defender-format alerts use alert tuning rules.

**Response actions** (from the identity page, advanced hunting or the Action center):
- **Disable** / **Enable**: AD, Entra ID and other connected identity sources
- **Revoke session**: Entra ID, Okta
- **Mark as compromised**: Entra ID
- **Force password change**: AD and Entra ID

**How actions run.** In AD, the sensor on a **domain controller** runs the action as the DC's **LocalSystem** account. Sensors on AD FS, AD CS or Entra Connect don't run remediation. In Entra ID, a Microsoft-managed *Microsoft Defender for Identity* app runs it. Analysts need the unified RBAC **Response (manage)** permission.

terms.d: Abusing directory replication to pull password hashes from a domain controller.
Reusing a stolen Kerberos ticket to authenticate as the victim.
Decoy account; any use of it raises an alert.

lessons.trap: Look for the category mapping (DCSync is credential access, pass-the-hash is lateral movement) and remember that only the DC sensor runs AD remediation.
lessons.example: An alert reports a workstation requesting replication from a domain controller. The analyst confirms DCSync, disables the account used and forces a password reset.

lessons.title: Microsoft Sentinel incidents in the Defender portal
lessons.short: After Microsoft Sentinel is onboarded to the Defender portal, SIEM and XDR incidents share one queue and one correlation engine. That changes how incident creation rules, automation rules and multi-workspace setups behave.
lessons.deep:
**Unified queue.** Sentinel analytics-rule alerts and Defender XDR alerts land in *Investigation & response > Incidents & alerts > Incidents* and are correlated across domains. Microsoft Sentinel is supported in the Azure portal only until **March 31, 2027**, after which it is Defender-portal only.

**What changes on onboarding.**
- **Microsoft incident creation rules** aren't supported and are **deactivated**, which prevents duplicate incidents.
- Incidents created in Sentinel by API, a Logic App or manually in the Azure portal **don't sync** to the Defender portal.
- Correlation can rename incidents, so automation rules should use the **analytics rule name** and **tags** as conditions, not incident titles. The incident provider condition and the `Description` field are removed.
- Automation rules with alert triggers act only on Sentinel alerts. Use the **Enhanced Alert Trigger** to include Defender XDR alerts.
- With several workspaces, only the **primary workspace** correlates with Defender XDR data.

**Correlation opt-out.** Add `#DONT_CORR#` at the start of an analytics rule description, or set Incident correlation to Disabled in the rule wizard, so the rule's alerts bypass correlation (the tenant default setting controls this).

**Investigating.** Analysts use the attack story, entity pages (with a **Sentinel events** tab), advanced hunting across XDR and workspace tables, and the `SecurityIncident` table. That table stores one row per update, so use `arg_max` to get the latest state.

terms.d: The one Sentinel workspace whose alerts correlate with Defender XDR data.
Description tag that excludes an analytics rule's alerts from Defender correlation.
Sentinel table that holds a row for each incident create or update.

lessons.trap: Don't build automation on incident titles after onboarding. Correlation can change them, so use analytics rule names and tags.
lessons.example: A SOC onboards two workspaces. Only the primary workspace's alerts join Defender XDR incidents, so alerts in the secondary workspace stay in their own incidents.

lessons.title: Embedded Security Copilot in the Defender portal
lessons.short: Security Copilot is embedded in the Defender portal. It summarizes incidents, suggests guided responses, explains scripts and files, summarizes devices and identities, writes KQL from natural language and drafts incident reports.
lessons.deep:
**Capabilities.**
- **Incident summary**: when and where the attack started, a timeline, assets, IoCs and threat actors. By default it is generated whenever an incident is opened (up to 100 alerts) and cached for a week. You can switch generation to severity-based or on demand.
- **Guided responses**, in four categories: **Triage** (classify as informational, true positive or false positive), **Containment**, **Investigation** (for example, contact the user in Teams) and **Remediation** (for example, view similar emails or incidents).
- **Script analysis**: explains suspicious PowerShell or other command lines.
- **File analysis**: explains what a file does.
- **Device summary** and **identity summary**.
- **Natural language to KQL** in advanced hunting.
- **Incident report**: writes up actions and findings for handover.

There is also a Copilot chat pane in the portal that is aware of the current page.

**Access and cost.** Users need provisioned access to Security Copilot, and each prompt consumes **Security Compute Units (SCUs)**. In 2026 Microsoft began including Security Copilot with Microsoft 365 E5, allocating SCUs per user licence. Grayed-out guided-response buttons mean the user's unified RBAC permissions don't allow that action.

terms.d: Security Compute Unit, the capacity that Security Copilot features consume.
Copilot recommendation cards for triage, containment, investigation and remediation.
Copilot explanation of a script or command line found in evidence.

lessons.trap: Copilot recommends actions but your RBAC still applies, so it can't run an action you aren't permitted to take.
lessons.example: An analyst opens a 40-alert incident, reads the Copilot summary, uses script analysis on an encoded PowerShell command and then follows the Containment card to isolate the device.

lessons.title: Agentic AI: Security Copilot agents in Defender
lessons.short: Security Copilot agents triage and investigate on their own, within the permissions you give them. In Defender, the Phishing Triage (Security Alert Triage) Agent gives verdicts on user-reported phishing and learns from analyst feedback written in plain language.
lessons.deep:
**Defender agents.**
- **Security Alert Triage Agent / Phishing Triage Agent**: triages *Email reported by user as malware or phish* alerts (and, in preview, some identity and cloud alerts). It gives a verdict with a natural-language rationale. **False positive** alerts are resolved, and **true positive** incidents stay open for an analyst.
- **Threat Intelligence Briefing Agent**: scheduled briefings on relevant threats.
- **Threat Hunting Assistant**: natural-language hunting that writes KQL and interprets results.
- **Security Analyst Agent**: no-code analyses such as anomaly detection and risk scoring.
- **Dynamic Threat Detection Agent**: an always-on backend service that finds false negatives and raises alerts mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.

**Phishing Triage prerequisites.** **Defender for Office 365 Plan 2**, Security Copilot SCUs, unified RBAC for MDO, reporting enabled in Outlook and the user-reported alert policy turned on. You must disable tuning rules that auto-resolve those alerts.

**Identity.** Agents run as a new **Microsoft Entra Agent ID** (recommended, least privilege) or as an existing user account.

**Oversight.** Incidents the agent worked carry an **Agent** tag. You can view the agent's activity and full workflow. To correct it, use **Change classification**, explain why, and select **Use this feedback to teach the agent**. Feedback that conflicts with earlier lessons is flagged as **Conflict**.

terms.d: AI that plans and runs multi-step tasks on its own, under human oversight.
Dedicated identity created for an agent, with only the permissions it needs.
Copilot agent that gives verdicts on user-reported phishing alerts.

lessons.trap: If an auto-resolve tuning rule still closes reported-phish alerts, the agent never sees them, so disable that rule first.
lessons.example: The agent marks a benefits-enrollment email as phishing. An analyst reclassifies it, explains that genuine mail comes from @benefits.contoso.com, and teaches the agent that lesson.

lessons.title: Investigating complex multi-stage, multi-domain attacks
lessons.short: Defender XDR correlates alerts from endpoints, identities, email, cloud apps and Sentinel into one multi-stage incident. Analysts use the attack story, incident merging, blast radius and identity alerts to follow lateral movement across domains.
lessons.deep:
**Correlation.** Defender groups alerts into one incident when they share entities (users, devices, mailboxes), artifacts (files, processes, senders), time frames or event sequences, for example a phishing click followed by a suspicious sign-in. Incidents are named automatically, for example *Multi-stage incident on multiple endpoints reported by multiple sources*.

**Merging.** When incidents are merged, Defender moves the alerts, tags and entities into the target incident. It closes the source incident and adds a **Redirected** tag. Automatic merge is blocked if one incident is **closed**, if they're assigned to **different people**, if they have **different classifications or determinations**, or if they contain devices in different device groups when that setting is on. Up to five incidents can be merged manually (preview).

**Attack story.** The incident graph can be replayed in time order, highlights the alerts related to an entity, and lets you take actions or run **Go hunt** queries. **Blast radius** (*View blast radius*) shows possible paths from a node to critical assets. Those paths are possibilities, not confirmed activity.

**Lateral movement.** Typical chain: initial access on a workstation, then credential dumping, then **pass-the-hash / pass-the-ticket / overpass-the-hash** to servers (Defender for Identity lateral movement alerts), then domain dominance (DCSync, Golden Ticket). Across domains, an AiTM phish (email) leads to token theft (Entra ID), then mailbox rules (Defender for Cloud Apps), then BEC.

terms.d: One incident that combines alerts from several attack stages and products.
Added to the source incident after it is merged into another.
Graph of possible propagation paths from a compromised node to critical targets.

lessons.trap: After a merge you can't choose the direction (Defender picks the target), and closed incidents are never merged automatically.
lessons.example: A Defender for Endpoint credential-dumping alert and a Defender for Identity pass-the-hash alert on the same account merge into a single incident that shows the path to a file server.

lessons.title: Managing incidents: status, assignment and classification
lessons.short: In the Defender portal you manage an incident from the Manage incident pane, where you set the owner, status, severity, tags, classification and comments. Every change is recorded in the Activities log.
lessons.deep:
**Status.** New incidents are **Active**. Set **In progress** while you work and **Resolved** when finished (a resolution note is required).

**Assignment.** New incidents have no owner. Only **one user or group** can own an incident, and assigning it also assigns all its alerts.

**Severity.** **High**, **Medium**, **Low** or **Informational**. It defaults to the **highest severity of its alerts** and can be changed.

**Classification.**
- **True positive**, with a threat type
- **Informational, expected activity**, for security tests, red team exercises or expected unusual behaviour
- **False positive**
- **Not set** (default)

**Tags.** System tags (red or black) mark the attack type, automatic actions (such as Attack Disruption) or Defender Experts involvement. Custom tags (white) are yours and can be used as queue filters.

**Comments and Activities.** Comments can be up to 30,000 characters. The **Activities** log records every user and system change and can be filtered by origin, provider, performed by and more.

**Naming.** Defender names incidents from alert attributes. You can rename an incident, but a later merge can overwrite the name.

The Defender portal is introducing an **incident cases** experience (preview) that builds on these same fields.

terms.d: Default status of a new Defender XDR incident.
Classification for real but authorized activity, such as red-team testing.
Audit trail of manual and automated changes made to an incident.

lessons.trap: Defender incidents start as Active. Sentinel (Azure portal) incidents and cases start as New, and exams mix the two.
lessons.example: A red-team exercise triggers credential-theft alerts. After verifying it with the red-team lead, the analyst resolves the incident as Informational, expected activity, with a security testing activity type.

lessons.title: Case management in the Microsoft Defender portal
lessons.short: Case management is a native ticketing experience in the Defender portal. A case groups related incidents, tasks, indicators, comments and attachments so SOC work that spans several incidents, or none, can be tracked without a third-party tool.
lessons.deep:
**Prerequisite.** A **Microsoft Sentinel workspace connected to the Defender portal**. Cases appear only in the Defender portal.

**Uses.** Investigations that span multiple incidents, threat-hunting projects, tracking IoCs or threat actors, and detection-tuning work.

**Case fields.** Case ID (auto-assigned from **1000**, never purged), priority (Very low to Critical), status (defaults **New**, **Open**, **Closed**; admins can add custom statuses), one assignee, description, due date and linked incidents.

**Tasks.** Each task has an owner, priority, due date, description and closing notes. Task statuses are New, In progress, Failed, Partially completed, Skipped and Completed.

**Linked objects.** Link incidents from the case or from an incident's menu. Link threat intelligence **indicators** (preview). Defender Threat Intelligence *Projects* are deprecated in favour of linking indicators to cases.

**Activity log and attachments.** Rich-text comments, automatic audit events, and file attachments that are scanned for malware (password-zip any samples).

**Permissions.**
- View: *Security data basics (read)* or **Microsoft Sentinel Reader**
- Create, assign, link and update: *Alerts (manage)* or **Microsoft Sentinel Responder**
- Customize statuses: *Core security settings (manage)* or **Microsoft Sentinel Contributor**

terms.d: Container that groups incidents, tasks, IoCs and evidence for one piece of SOC work.
Assigned unit of work inside a case, with its own status and closing notes.
Admin-defined case status, such as Research phase.

lessons.trap: Case management needs Sentinel connected to the Defender portal and isn't available in the Azure portal. Responder can manage cases, but only Contributor can customize statuses.
lessons.example: A hunter opens a case for a suspected threat actor, links three incidents and five IoCs, and assigns containment tasks to the IR team with due dates.

lessons.title: Investigate device timelines
lessons.short: The device timeline in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint lists every process, file, network, registry and logon event on one device in time order. You search, filter, flag events, view MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and pivot to advanced hunting.
lessons.deep:
Every onboarded device has a device page; its **Timeline** tab is the EDR sensor's raw story of what happened on that machine.

- **Default range:** the past **30 days**. Change it with the date picker or the calendar icon (past day, week, 30 days, custom range), or highlight part of the time bar.
- **Filters:** choose the **Data type** (events or techniques), event groups and **Flagged events**. Flag the events that matter (flag icon in the Flag column) so you can rebuild the attack sequence later.
- **Techniques:** events mapped to MITRE ATT&CK appear in **bold with a blue icon**; the technique ID and name show under **Additional information**.
- **Event details:** selecting an event opens a side panel with a related-entity graph and process tree. **Hunt for related events** opens advanced hunting with that event plus other events on the same device around the same time (from a technique pane, the technique itself is not returned).
- **Export:** the current date or a range of up to **seven days** per export.
- **Firewall events** (5025, 5031, 5157) appear only if the *Audit Filtering Platform Connection* audit policy is on.

For longer or cross-device work, switch to advanced hunting tables such as `DeviceProcessEvents`.

terms.d: Chronological list of sensor events and alerts for a single device in Defender for Endpoint.
Events you mark with the flag icon so you can filter the timeline down to them.
Button that opens advanced hunting with the selected event and nearby events on the same device.
A timeline entry mapped to a MITRE ATT&CK technique, shown bold with a blue icon.

lessons.trap: Exams test limits: the timeline shows 30 days by default and exports at most seven days at a time; it is not where you change retention.
lessons.example: An analyst flags the PowerShell download, the new scheduled task and the outbound connection on a laptop, then filters to Flagged events to brief the incident lead.

lessons.title: Device response actions and investigation packages
lessons.short: From the device page you can isolate, contain, restrict app execution, run an antivirus scan, or collect an investigation package. Each action needs a comment and is tracked in the Action center.
lessons.deep:
Device response actions sit on the device page action bar in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.

- **Isolate device:** cuts the device off the network but keeps it connected to the Defender service. **Full** isolation blocks everything; **selective** isolation (Windows 10 1709+) can keep **Outlook and Microsoft Teams** working so you can still talk to the user. **Release from isolation** undoes it.
- **Contain device:** for a device that is *not onboarded* (found by device discovery). Every onboarded device blocks traffic to and from it. Undo with **Release from containment**.
- **Restrict app execution:** applies a code integrity policy so only **Microsoft-signed** files run (Windows 10 1709+, Windows 11, Server 2019+).
- **Run antivirus scan:** choose **Quick** or **Full**; works even when Defender Antivirus is in passive mode.
- **Collect investigation package:** a zip of forensic data: Autoruns (ASEP registry keys), installed programs, network connections (ARP, DNS cache, firewall log), Prefetch files, processes, scheduled tasks, the Security event log, services, SMB sessions, temp directories, users and groups, and a CollectionSummaryReport.

**Licensing:** Plan 1 offers only Run antivirus scan, Isolate device, Stop and quarantine a file, and file indicators; the rest need **Plan 2**. Isolation needs the **Active remediation actions** permission. Every action, with who submitted it and whether it worked, is listed in the **Action center**.

terms.d: Isolation that still lets Outlook and Teams communicate so the analyst can reach the user.
Makes all onboarded devices block communication with a discovered but unmanaged device.
Code integrity policy allowing only Microsoft-signed files to run.
Forensic zip (autoruns, prefetch, processes, event log, network data) collected from a device.

lessons.trap: Isolate works on onboarded devices; Contain targets unmanaged devices. Restrict app execution allows only Microsoft-signed code, not your own approved list.
lessons.example: Ransomware is spreading from a laptop: the analyst selectively isolates it, keeps Teams open to call the user, and collects an investigation package for forensics.

lessons.title: Live response sessions
lessons.short: Live response gives an analyst a remote shell on a device through Defender for Endpoint to collect files, inspect processes, run library scripts and remediate. Basic and advanced commands are split by RBAC permission.
lessons.deep:
**Live response** opens a cloud-brokered remote shell on an onboarded device: no VPN or RDP needed.

**Turn it on** in Settings > Endpoints > **Advanced features**: *Live response*, *Live response for servers* (separate toggle), and optionally *Live response unsigned script execution* (only signed PowerShell scripts run otherwise).

**Permissions:** RBAC roles grant **basic** or **advanced** live response.
- Basic commands: `cd`, `dir`, `processes`, `connections`, `registry`, `scheduledtasks`, `services`, `persistence`, `fileinfo`, `findfile`, `getfile`, `jobs`, `fg`.
- Advanced commands: `run` (script from the **library**), `putfile` (copy a library file to the device), `library`, `analyze`, `remediate`, `undo`, plus `scan`, `isolate`, `collect` on some platforms.

**Syntax worth knowing:** `run script.ps1 -parameters "-Name x"`; `putfile tool.exe -keep` keeps the file after restart (default is deleted); `-overwrite` replaces it; add `&` to send a download to the background and `fg <command ID>` to bring it back.

**Limits:** 5 sessions per user, one session per device, 50 concurrent sessions per tenant, 30 minutes idle timeout, `getfile` up to 3 GB. Every command is recorded on the **Command log** tab. Ctrl+C cancels only in the portal; the agent may keep running the command.

terms.d: Store of scripts and files that run and putfile can use on devices.
Permission level that unlocks run, putfile, remediate, analyze and similar commands.
Basic command that downloads a file from the device (up to 3 GB).
Session tab recording every command, its duration and status.

lessons.trap: Running scripts needs advanced permission AND the script in the library; unsigned scripts need the separate unsigned-script setting.
lessons.example: An analyst connects to a server, lists persistence entries, downloads a suspicious DLL with getfile, then runs a signed cleanup script from the library.

lessons.title: Evidence and Response in an incident
lessons.short: The Evidence and Response tab of a Defender XDR incident lists every entity analyzed from its alerts, such as files, processes, IP addresses and emails, with a verdict and a remediation status you can act on.
lessons.deep:
When alerts from Defender for Endpoint are grouped into an incident, the incident page shows them from several angles:

- **Attack story:** alerts plus an incident graph you can replay.
- **Alerts:** the related alerts and why they were linked.
- **Assets:** devices, users, mailboxes, apps and cloud resources involved.
- **Evidence and Response:** every **evidence** item (files, processes, services, IP addresses, URLs, emails, registry values) analyzed from the alerts.

Each evidence item gets a **verdict**: **Malicious**, **Suspicious** or **Clean**, and a **remediation status**. Items with status **Pending approval** can be **approved or rejected** straight from the tab, and you can open the entity or **Go hunt** for related activity. Approved actions then appear in the **Action center**, where completed actions can also be undone.

Why it matters: evidence is the list of *things* (not events) you must clean up before you can close the incident. A device is not clean until every malicious file, persistence item and process on it is remediated.

Note: Microsoft is moving from the classic incident page to **incident cases** (preview), but the evidence and verdict concepts stay the same.

terms.d: An entity such as a file, process, IP or email analyzed as part of an incident.
Malicious, Suspicious or Clean result assigned to an evidence item.
Remediation status of an action waiting for an analyst to approve or reject it.
Portal page listing pending and completed remediation actions across Defender.

lessons.trap: Verdicts are Malicious/Suspicious/Clean; True positive/False positive are alert classifications, a different field.
lessons.example: An incident shows a malicious DLL with Pending approval; the analyst approves quarantine from Evidence and Response and confirms success in the Action center.

lessons.title: File, IP and other entity pages
lessons.short: Entity pages show an object across the whole organization. The file page shows prevalence and offers Stop and quarantine, indicators, download and deep analysis; the IP view shows which devices talked to an address.
lessons.deep:
Entity investigation means stepping out of one device to ask: *where else is this?*

**File page** (open from an alert, the timeline or search): file details and PE metadata, related incidents and alerts, **prevalence** (devices in the last 30 days, VirusTotal ratio, Defender Antivirus detection), all observed file names, and devices where it was seen. Actions:
- **Stop and quarantine file:** stops running processes, quarantines the file and removes persistence on devices that saw it in the last **30 days**. Up to **1,000 devices**; offline devices get 3 days to come back.
- **Add indicator** (Manage indicator): block a PE file by hash across the fleet, persistently. Use it for larger scopes or offline machines.
- **Download/Collect file:** password-protected zip for analysis.
- **Deep analysis:** detonates a **PE file** (.exe, .dll) in a Microsoft cloud **sandbox** and reports behaviors such as contacted IPs, dropped files and registry changes.

**IP address view:** geolocation/ASN details, related alerts, devices that connected to it (list capped at **100 devices**), and prevalence (default **30 days**). Domains and URLs have similar views. **User** pages show related alerts, devices logged on and identity risk.

terms.d: How widely a file or IP has been seen inside (and outside) the organization.
Stops processes, quarantines the file and deletes persistence on devices that had it.
Cloud sandbox detonation of a PE file producing a behavior report.
Hash-based allow or block rule applied across onboarded devices.

lessons.trap: Stop and quarantine is limited to 1,000 devices and recently seen files; for wide or persistent blocking the answer is an indicator.
lessons.example: A dropper appears on 12 laptops: the analyst runs Stop and quarantine, submits it for deep analysis, and adds a block indicator so it cannot run again.

lessons.title: Incidents from automatic attack disruption
lessons.short: Automatic attack disruption correlates XDR signals into a high-confidence incident and contains attacker-controlled assets automatically, for example contain device, contain user or disable user. Analysts review the tagged incident, finish the investigation, then release assets.
lessons.deep:
**Automatic attack disruption** is Defender XDR's built-in, incident-level response to attacks such as ransomware and business email compromise. When signals from endpoints, identities, email and SaaS form a high-confidence incident, Defender acts in real time without waiting for an analyst.

**Endpoint-related actions (Defender for Endpoint):**
- **Contain device:** all onboarded devices block communication with the compromised device.
- **Contain IP:** blocks an IP tied to non-onboarded devices.
- **Contain user:** onboarded devices block the user's network logons, RPC, SMB and RDP. It does **not** disable the account in the identity provider.
Other products add **Disable user** (Defender for Identity on domain controllers, by default via the **LocalSystem** action account), **Revoke session**, and OAuth app actions.

**Prerequisites for endpoints:** device discovery set to **Standard discovery** (for contain device) and a device-group automation level of **Full** (recommended). It works whether Defender Antivirus is Active, Passive or EDR block mode.

**Responding:** the incident carries the **Attack Disruption** tag and a banner; assets show labels such as *contained*. Review actions in the incident and the **Action center**, or hunt `DisruptionAndResponseEvents`. After you finish investigating, undo with **Release from containment** or **Enable user**. Critical assets can be excluded beforehand.

terms.d: Incident tag showing that automatic attack disruption acted on it.
Onboarded devices block a compromised account's network logons; the account stays enabled.
Device discovery mode required for automatic contain device.
Advanced hunting table of disruption and response actions across the org.

lessons.trap: Contain user is not the same as disabling the account; releasing assets is done from the incident or Action center, not by deleting the incident.
lessons.example: Ransomware moves from a file server; disruption contains the server and the stolen admin account. The analyst confirms cleanup, then releases both from the incident page.

lessons.title: Microsoft Purview Audit (Standard) and audit search
lessons.short: Microsoft Purview Audit records user and admin activity across Microsoft 365 in the unified audit log. You search it in the Purview portal as search jobs, or with Search-UnifiedAuditLog in Exchange Online PowerShell.
lessons.deep:
The **unified audit log** captures activity from Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, Microsoft Entra ID and many other services. **Audit (Standard)** is on by default for most Microsoft 365 subscriptions and keeps records for **180 days**.

**Searching in the Purview portal (Audit):** each search is a **search job** that keeps running if you close the browser.
- Criteria: date range (UTC, up to **180 days**), keyword, admin units, activities (friendly names or exact **operation names**), **record types**, users, file/folder/site, workloads.
- Up to **10** search jobs in parallel per user; completed jobs are kept for **30 days**.
- Export up to **50,000** rows (Standard) or 1,000,000 (Premium).
- Events from core services usually appear **60 to 90 minutes** after they happen.

**Permissions:** the **Audit Logs** or **View-Only Audit Logs** role.

**PowerShell:** `Search-UnifiedAuditLog` (Exchange Online PowerShell) needs `-StartDate` and `-EndDate`; filter with `-UserIds`, `-Operations`, `-RecordType`, `-IPAddresses`, `-ObjectIds`, `-FreeText`. `-ResultSize` defaults to 100 and maxes at **5,000** per call; use `-SessionId` with `-SessionCommand ReturnLargeSet` to page up to 50,000. The details are in the JSON `AuditData` property.

Threat hunting uses: new inbox rules (`New-InboxRule`), mailbox permission grants, file downloads, admin role changes.

terms.d: Central Microsoft 365 log of user and admin activities across workloads.
Asynchronous audit search in the Purview portal; results kept 30 days.
Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlet that queries the unified audit log.
JSON property holding the detailed fields of an audit record.

lessons.trap: Audit (Standard) keeps 180 days, not 90; and freshly generated events can take 60-90 minutes to become searchable.
lessons.example: An analyst searches the last 30 days for New-InboxRule operations by a suspected compromised user and exports the results to CSV.

lessons.title: Audit (Premium) and mailbox forensics
lessons.short: Audit (Premium) adds longer retention and intelligent insight events such as Send, SearchQueryInitiatedExchange and SearchQueryInitiatedSharePoint. MailItemsAccessed shows which mail an attacker read, through Bind and Sync records.
lessons.deep:
**Audit (Premium)** builds on Standard for users with the right **E5 (or add-on) license** and the **Microsoft 365 Advanced Auditing** app enabled.

**Retention:** Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive and Entra ID records are kept **1 year** by default; custom audit retention policies up to 1 year, or **10 years** with the *10-Year Audit Log Retention* add-on. Retention policies are **not retroactive**.

**Intelligent insights (crucial events):**
- **Send**: the user sent, replied to or forwarded a message.
- **SearchQueryInitiatedExchange / SearchQueryInitiatedSharePoint**: what a user searched for. These must be switched on per mailbox: `Set-Mailbox <user> -AuditOwner @{Add="SearchQueryInitiated"}`.
- Teams events such as MessageSent and MessageRead with extra properties.

**MailItemsAccessed** (now part of Audit Standard for E3/E5 users) is the key compromise event:
- **Bind**: one specific message accessed, identified by `InternetMessageId` (binds in a 2-minute window are grouped).
- **Sync**: a whole folder was synced (Outlook desktop); assume **every item in that folder** was accessed.
Match `ClientIPAddress`, `ClientInfoString` and `SessionId` to the attacker to scope what was read.

terms.d: Licensed audit tier with 1-year default retention, 10-year option and intelligent insights.
Audit event recording mailbox reads, as Bind (message) or Sync (folder).
Premium event logging a user's Outlook search terms; enabled with Set-Mailbox -AuditOwner.
Premium event logged when a user sends, replies to or forwards mail.

lessons.trap: Search query events are not on by default; and a Sync record means the whole folder is treated as compromised.
lessons.example: After an AiTM phish, MailItemsAccessed Bind records from the attacker's IP list the InternetMessageIds of the invoices the attacker opened.

lessons.title: Content search in Microsoft Purview eDiscovery
lessons.short: Content search now runs inside Microsoft Purview eDiscovery: you create a search in a case (or the system Content Search case), add data sources, build a KeyQL query, then review statistics and samples before export.
lessons.deep:
The classic Content search tool was retired on **31 August 2025**; searches now live in the **new eDiscovery** experience in the Microsoft Purview portal. A system-generated **Content Search** case holds content searches, and you can also create searches in any eDiscovery case.

**Workflow:** eDiscovery > **Cases** > open case > **Searches** > **Create a search** > add **data sources** (Exchange mailboxes, SharePoint sites, OneDrive, Teams, Microsoft 365 Groups, Viva Engage) > build the query with the **condition builder** or the **KeyQL** editor (Copilot can draft KeyQL) > **Run query** > view **Statistics** or a **Sample**.

**KeyQL rules a security analyst needs:** `from:` / `to:` / `subject:"exact phrase"` / `kind:email`; no space after the colon; AND, OR, NOT, NEAR must be **uppercase**; only prefix wildcards (`invoic*`); searches use UTC; an empty query returns everything.

**After the search:** **Export** results (standard), or **Add to review set** for analytics (premium).

**Roles:** the **eDiscovery Manager** role group (managers see their own cases; **eDiscovery Administrators** see all). **Compliance Search** lets you search and see estimates; **Preview** and **Export** are separate roles.

Security use: find every copy of a phishing email or leaked file across mailboxes and sites.

terms.d: Keyword Query Language used for eDiscovery search queries.
UI for adding keyword and property conditions to an eDiscovery search.
Estimated item counts, sizes and top locations for a search.
Premium eDiscovery copy of results for tagging, analytics and review.

lessons.trap: Content search is in Purview eDiscovery, not Threat Explorer or Audit; and Boolean operators must be uppercase in KeyQL.
lessons.example: An analyst searches all mailboxes for subject:"Payroll update" from an external sender, checks statistics to see 214 hits, then exports a report.

lessons.title: Search and purge malicious email
lessons.short: After a content search finds a malicious or spilled email, an authorized user can purge it with New-ComplianceSearchAction -Purge, using SoftDelete or HardDelete. It needs the Search And Purge role and has strict per-mailbox limits.
lessons.deep:
**Search and purge** turns an eDiscovery search into a deletion. It is an incident-response tool, not a mailbox clean-up tool.

**Roles:** searching needs **eDiscovery Manager** or the **Compliance Search** role. Purging needs the **Search And Purge** role, which is in the Purview **Organization Management** role group (Exchange Online Organization Management is not enough).

**Steps (Security & Compliance PowerShell):**
1. `Connect-IPPSSession -EnableSearchOnlySession`
2. `New-ComplianceSearch -Name "Remove Phish" -ExchangeLocation All -ContentMatchQuery '(Subject:"Action required")'` then `Start-ComplianceSearch`
3. Check the item count (`Get-ComplianceSearch`) to confirm scope.
4. `New-ComplianceSearchAction -SearchName "Remove Phish" -Purge -PurgeType SoftDelete` (or `HardDelete`)
5. `Get-ComplianceSearchAction -Identity "Remove Phish_Purge"` to check status.

**SoftDelete** moves items to Recoverable Items (Deletions), where users can recover them; **HardDelete** marks them for permanent removal.

**Limits:** **10 items per mailbox** per run (100 with premium/Graph), up to 50,000 mailboxes per search, Exchange Online mailboxes and public folders only, unindexed items are skipped, held items are preserved. With **Defender for Office 365 Plan 2**, Microsoft recommends Threat Explorer remediation instead.

terms.d: Role that allows deleting items found by a compliance search.
Cmdlet that runs an action such as -Purge on a completed search.
Purge type moving items to Recoverable Items, still recoverable by the user.
Purge type marking items for permanent removal.

lessons.trap: eDiscovery Manager can search but cannot purge; the -Purge parameter is missing without the Search And Purge role.
lessons.example: A phishing message reached 300 mailboxes in an E3 tenant; the analyst runs a scoped search, confirms the count, and soft-deletes the messages.

lessons.title: Microsoft Graph activity logs
lessons.short: Microsoft Graph activity logs record every HTTP request to Microsoft Graph in your tenant: which app or user, which URI, method and response. Stream them with Entra diagnostic settings to Log Analytics and hunt with KQL.
lessons.deep:
Attackers who steal tokens or consent to rogue apps often use **Microsoft Graph** to read mail, enumerate users or change groups. **Microsoft Graph activity logs** give you an audit trail of **every API request** Graph receives for your tenant, including requests from line-of-business apps, SDKs, AI clients and Microsoft apps.

**Prerequisites:** a **Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2** license, an Azure subscription, and an admin role; **Security Administrator** is the least-privileged role that can configure the diagnostic setting.

**Enable:** create a **diagnostic setting** that sends the logs to a **Log Analytics workspace** (KQL hunting, Microsoft Sentinel), an **Azure Storage account** (long-term retention) or **Event Hubs** (third-party SIEM). You pay for the Azure resources used.

**Table:** `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs`. Key columns: `RequestUri`, `RequestMethod`, `ResponseStatusCode`, `AppId`, `ServicePrincipalId`, `UserId`, `IPAddress`, `UserAgent`, `Scopes`, `Roles`, `SignInActivityId`.

**Hunting ideas:** spikes of 401/403 responses, risky users calling Graph (join `AADRiskyUsers`), unusual apps reading `/messages`. Correlate with sign-in logs by joining `SignInActivityId` to `UniqueTokenIdentifier`.

**Latency:** usually within 30 minutes, sometimes up to 2 hours. Defender XDR advanced hunting offers a similar `GraphAPIAuditEvents` table.

terms.d: Log Analytics table containing Microsoft Graph API request records.
Azure Monitor configuration that streams logs to a workspace, storage or Event Hubs.
Graph log column that joins to UniqueTokenIdentifier in sign-in logs.
Identifier of the app identity that made the request.

lessons.trap: Graph activity logs need Entra ID P1/P2 and must be streamed via diagnostic settings; they are not in the Purview audit log or on by default.
lessons.example: After a consent-phishing alert, an analyst queries MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs for the app's AppId and finds thousands of GET requests to users' /messages.

lessons.title: Choosing the right advanced hunting table
lessons.short: Advanced hunting in Microsoft Defender XDR stores telemetry in named tables grouped by source: Device* for endpoints, Email* for mail, Identity* for Active Directory, CloudAppEvents for SaaS, and AlertInfo/AlertEvidence for alerts. Picking the right table is the first step of every hunt.
lessons.deep:
Every advanced hunting query starts with a table name. The schema is organised by where the data comes from:
- **Endpoints (Defender for Endpoint):** `DeviceProcessEvents` (process creation, command lines), `DeviceNetworkEvents` (connections), `DeviceFileEvents` (file create/modify), `DeviceRegistryEvents` (registry changes), `DeviceLogonEvents` (sign-ins on devices), `DeviceImageLoadEvents` (DLL loads), `DeviceEvents` (antivirus, exploit protection and other security control events), `DeviceInfo` (machine details).
- **Email (Defender for Office 365):** `EmailEvents` (delivery and blocking), `EmailAttachmentInfo`, `EmailUrlInfo`, `EmailPostDeliveryEvents` (actions after delivery such as ZAP), `UrlClickEvents` (Safe Links clicks).
- **Identity (Defender for Identity):** `IdentityLogonEvents`, `IdentityQueryEvents` (LDAP/AD object queries), `IdentityDirectoryEvents` (domain controller events).
- **Cloud apps:** `CloudAppEvents`.
- **Entra sign-ins:** `EntraIdSignInEvents` (interactive and non-interactive; replaces `AADSignInEventsBeta`, needs Entra ID P2) and `EntraIdSpnSignInEvents` for service principals.
- **Alerts:** `AlertInfo` (one row per alert) and `AlertEvidence` (entities attached to alerts), joined on `AlertId`.
- **Exposure Management:** `ExposureGraphNodes` and `ExposureGraphEdges`.

terms.d: Endpoint table of process creation events, including FileName and ProcessCommandLine.
Table of files, IPs, URLs, users and devices associated with alerts; joins to AlertInfo on AlertId.
Defender for Identity table of queries for AD objects such as users, groups and devices (LDAP, SAMR, DNS).
Safe Links click events from email, Teams and Office apps.

lessons.trap: The exam offers near-identical table names: DeviceEvents (security control events) versus DeviceProcessEvents (process launches), or EmailUrlInfo (URLs in mail) versus UrlClickEvents (actual clicks).
lessons.example: To find who clicked a phishing link, query UrlClickEvents; to see which device then launched powershell.exe, pivot to DeviceProcessEvents.

lessons.title: KQL fundamentals for hunting
lessons.short: Kusto Query Language (KQL) pipes a table through operators with `|`: `where` filters rows, `project` picks columns, `extend` adds calculated columns, `summarize` aggregates with `by`, and `top`/`order by` rank results. `ago()` builds relative time filters.
lessons.deep:
A KQL query reads top to bottom: a table, then operators separated by the pipe `|`, each working on the output of the previous one.
- `where Timestamp > ago(7d)`: filter rows; `ago()` subtracts a timespan from now (`1h`, `7d`).
- String operators: `==` is case-sensitive equality, `=~` is case-insensitive; `has` matches a whole term and uses the term index (fast); `contains` matches any substring (slower); `startswith`, `in~ (...)` and `matches regex` also exist.
- `project`: keep (and optionally rename) only the listed columns. `project-away` drops columns.
- `extend`: add a calculated column while keeping all existing ones, for example `extend Hour = hourofday(Timestamp)`.
- `summarize count() by AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)`: aggregate; `bin()` rounds time into buckets. Without `by`, summarize returns one row.
- `top 10 by Count desc`, `order by`, `take` (any N rows), `distinct`.
Defender XDR tables use the `Timestamp` column; Microsoft Sentinel tables use `TimeGenerated`. All advanced hunting data is in UTC. Filter early on time and indexed terms to keep queries inside quotas.

terms.d: `has` matches whole terms using the index; `contains` matches any substring and is slower.
Adds calculated columns while keeping all existing columns.
Rounds values (often time) down to fixed-size buckets for summarize.
Case-insensitive string equality.

lessons.trap: Candidates swap project and extend: project removes every column you don't list, extend keeps them all and adds new ones.
lessons.example: `DeviceLogonEvents | where ActionType == 'LogonFailed' | summarize count() by AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)` reveals password-spray bursts per hour.

lessons.title: KQL patterns to identify threats
lessons.short: Real hunts correlate data: `join` links tables on a shared column, `let` names reusable values, `arg_max()` returns the latest row per entity, `make_set()` collects distinct values, and functions such as `FileProfile()` enrich hashes with prevalence data.
lessons.deep:
Threat patterns rarely sit in one table, so hunters combine data:
- `join kind=... (OtherTable) on Column`: the default kind is **innerunique** (deduplicates the left side). `inner` keeps all matches, `leftouter` keeps unmatched left rows, `leftanti` returns left rows with NO match (great for 'never seen before' logic), `leftsemi` returns matched left rows only.
- `union`: stack rows from several tables; schemas do not have to match.
- `let Name = ...;` defines a variable, list or sub-query; each `let` ends with a semicolon.
- `summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId`: the most recent full row per device. `arg_min` gives the earliest.
- `make_set(x)` / `make_list(x)`: arrays of distinct / all values; `dcount(x)` counts distinct values; `mv-expand` turns array elements back into rows.
- `invoke FileProfile(SHA1, 1000)`: an advanced hunting function that adds GlobalPrevalence, signer and other file details. Others include `DeviceFromIP()` and `AssignedIPAddresses()`.
Example: join EmailAttachmentInfo to DeviceFileEvents on `SHA256` to see attachments that landed on disk.

terms.d: Default KQL join kind; deduplicates left-side keys before matching.
Join kind returning only left rows with no match on the right.
Aggregation returning the row with the maximum value of an expression, e.g. latest Timestamp.
Advanced hunting function invoked to enrich file hashes with prevalence and signer info.

lessons.trap: Expect a join-kind question: leftanti (no match) versus leftsemi (match only) versus leftouter (all left rows).
lessons.example: A hunter lists rare binaries by taking distinct SHA1 values from DeviceProcessEvents, invoking FileProfile and keeping GlobalPrevalence < 50.

lessons.title: Creating advanced hunting queries
lessons.short: Advanced hunting (Investigation & response > Hunting > Advanced hunting) offers guided mode, a query builder for KQL beginners, and advanced mode for hand-written KQL. Native Defender data goes back 30 days; queries return up to 100,000 rows and time out after 10 minutes.
lessons.deep:
Open the Microsoft Defender portal and go to **Investigation & response > Hunting > Advanced hunting**.
- **Guided mode:** build queries by picking a domain, conditions and filters, no KQL required.
- **Advanced mode:** write KQL from scratch with schema browser, IntelliSense and sample queries.
Save queries to **My queries** or **Shared queries** so the team can reuse them; queries from threat analytics reports can be opened directly here.
**Quotas (per query):** 30 days of native Defender XDR data, 100,000 rows, 64 MB result size, 10-minute timeout. CPU use is metered per tenant every 15 minutes; heavy users see warnings and can be blocked until the next cycle.
**Sentinel in the Defender portal:** onboarded workspace tables appear in the same schema and follow the workspace's analytics-tier retention, which is how you hunt Defender data older than 30 days. Data that lives only in the Sentinel data lake tier is not queryable here; use data lake exploration instead.
All times are UTC. Event data appears almost immediately; entity data such as DeviceInfo updates hourly.
Access: Security Reader, Security Administrator, Global Reader (Entra) or Unified RBAC 'Security data basics (read)'.

terms.d: Query builder in advanced hunting for users not yet fluent in KQL.
Advanced hunting editor for writing KQL directly.
Saved advanced hunting queries visible to others in the tenant.

lessons.trap: The exam tests limits: 30 days of native data, 100,000 rows, 10 minutes; longer retention needs a Sentinel workspace, not a setting in Defender.
lessons.example: A junior analyst uses guided mode to filter EmailEvents by sender domain, then switches to advanced mode to see and tweak the generated KQL.

lessons.title: Turning hunting queries into custom detections
lessons.short: A good hunting query can become a custom detection rule that runs on a schedule (Continuous/NRT, every 1, 3, 12 or 24 hours) and raises alerts. Results must include Timestamp and ReportId plus an entity column such as DeviceId for actions like isolation.
lessons.deep:
From the advanced hunting editor select **Create detection rule**. The wizard asks for alert details (name, frequency, severity, category, MITRE techniques), impacted entities, response actions and scope.
**Required columns:** project `Timestamp` (or `TimeGenerated`) and `ReportId` from the same event. For Device* tables also include `DeviceId`. Aggregated queries can keep these with `summarize (Timestamp, ReportId) = arg_max(Timestamp, ReportId), count() by DeviceId`.
**Frequency and lookback (Defender data):** every 24 hours = 30 days; every 12 hours = 48 hours; every 3 hours = 12 hours; every hour = 4 hours. **Continuous (NRT)** works only when the query uses a single table, supported operators, and no joins, unions or externaldata. **Custom** frequency (5 minutes to 14 days) is for Sentinel-only data.
**Actions:** devices (isolate, collect investigation package, antivirus scan, initiate investigation, restrict app execution, needs DeviceId), files (quarantine, allow/block), users (mark compromised, disable, reset authentication), email (move or delete, needs NetworkMessageId and RecipientEmailAddress).
Each rule raises at most 150 alerts per run. Creating rules on Defender data needs Security settings (manage) or Security Administrator.

terms.d: Saved advanced hunting query that runs on a schedule and generates alerts and optional actions.
Event identifier column that, with Timestamp, lets the rule locate the triggering event.
Near-real-time custom detection frequency for single-table queries without joins or unions.

lessons.trap: Missing DeviceId or ReportId in the projected output is the classic reason a rule can't be saved or can't isolate devices.
lessons.example: A hunt for repeated antivirus detections becomes an hourly rule that automatically collects an investigation package from each matching DeviceId.

lessons.title: Interpreting threat analytics
lessons.short: Threat analytics in the Defender portal is Microsoft's in-product threat intelligence: reports on actors, campaigns, tools, techniques and vulnerabilities, each showing related incidents, impacted assets, exposure and recommended actions for YOUR tenant.
lessons.deep:
Threat analytics (dashboard at security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3) is written by Microsoft security researchers and also surfaces curated OSINT.
**Dashboard:** *Latest threats* (recently published or updated), *High-impact threats* (most active and resolved alerts in your tenant), *Highest exposure threats* (based on vulnerability severity and how many of your devices could be exploited).
**Report types:** Activity (a campaign), Actor (a tracked threat actor's motives, targets, TTPs), Tool, Technique, Vulnerability (CVEs), Core threat, and OSINT.
**Report tabs:** Overview (charts of active vs resolved alerts), Analyst report (executive summary, technical overview, MITRE ATT&CK techniques observed, **Detections/Hunting queries** vetted by Microsoft analysts, recommendations, references), Related incidents, Impacted assets (distinct assets with at least one active alert), Endpoints exposure, Recommended actions, and Indicators.
Hunting queries can be run in advanced hunting or turned into custom detections.
**Access:** a Defender product licence (Defender for Endpoint P1 alone is not enough). 'Security data basics (read)' shows reports and incidents; 'Vulnerability management (read)' and 'Exposure Management (read)' show exposure and recommended actions. Email notifications can be configured for report updates.

terms.d: Threat analytics report on a Microsoft-tracked threat actor's motivations, targets and TTPs.
Dashboard list ranking threats by vulnerability severity and number of exploitable devices.
Report tab showing devices vulnerable to the threat and missing mitigations.

lessons.trap: Know which tab answers which question: incidents in your tenant (Related incidents), vulnerable devices (Endpoints exposure), KQL to hunt (Analyst report).
lessons.example: After a ransomware advisory, the SOC opens its threat analytics report, checks Related incidents for activity and Endpoints exposure for unpatched servers.

lessons.title: Hunting graphs in advanced hunting
lessons.short: The hunting graph in Defender advanced hunting renders relationships as nodes (devices, users, IPs, cloud resources) and edges (permissions, logons, routes). Predefined scenarios such as 'Attack paths to critical asset' or 'Paths between two entities' run without writing KQL.
lessons.deep:
Tables are poor at showing chains like 'user can authenticate as service principal, which has a role on a key vault'. The **hunting graph** draws those chains.
**Open it:** Investigation & response > Hunting > Advanced hunting, then select the hunting graph icon or **Create new > Hunting graph**. A tab named *New graph* opens.
**Predefined scenarios** (prebuilt queries, filterable by MITRE technique) include Attack paths to critical asset, Entity relationship map, Paths between two entities, Access to key vaults, Users with access to sensitive data, Choke points to SQL data stores, OAuth applications with privileged access, Paths to domain admins and Kerberoast paths to critical assets.
**Filters:** Show only the shortest paths; source node (is critical, is vulnerable, exposed to the internet); target node (has sensitive data); edge type (has permissions to, can authenticate as, member of, routes traffic to...) and edge direction.
Select nodes and edges for details, expand or focus on entities.
**Prerequisites:** a role for advanced hunting, an onboarded Microsoft Sentinel data lake (the graph is auto-provisioned), and at least read access in Microsoft Security Exposure Management.

terms.d: A graph entity such as a device, user account, IP address or cloud resource.
A relationship between nodes, for example 'has permissions to' or 'can authenticate as'.
A node that appears in many paths to critical assets; fixing it breaks many paths.

lessons.trap: The hunting graph lives in advanced hunting; blast radius lives on the incident graph. Both need the Sentinel data lake and Exposure Management read access.
lessons.example: A hunter runs 'Access to key vaults' for a production vault and finds a guest account with an indirect path through a group membership.

lessons.title: Blast radius analysis
lessons.short: Blast radius on the Defender incident graph shows possible propagation paths from a compromised node to critical assets. Select a node and choose View blast radius; the top eight paths load first.
lessons.deep:
Blast radius combines pre-breach exposure data with post-breach incident data. It is built on the Microsoft Sentinel data lake and graph and extends and replaces the older attack path view in incidents.
**How to use it:** open an incident from the Incidents page, select a node on the incident graph, then **View blast radius** (the menu shows 'No blast radius found' if none exist). The graph loads the eight top-rated attack paths; **View full blast radius list** shows all paths and targets.
