questions.explain: Boolean operators in KeyQL must be uppercase, so AND NOT excludes the sender. Lowercase not is treated as a keyword, NEAR finds terms close together, and OR would broaden the results instead of excluding hr@contoso.com.

questions.stem: You are using Microsoft Purview eDiscovery to locate a malicious attachment across Exchange mailboxes. Put the steps in order.
options: Open an eDiscovery case and select Create a search on the Searches tab
Add the Exchange mailboxes as data sources
Build the query with the condition builder or KeyQL
Run the query and review the statistics and sample
Export the results or a report
questions.explain: Searches are created inside a case, then you add data sources, define the query, run it and check statistics and samples to confirm scope, and finally export results or a report for further investigation.

questions.stem: An analyst is a member of the eDiscovery Manager subgroup. A colleague created an eDiscovery case and did not add the analyst. What can the analyst do with that case?
options: Nothing: eDiscovery Managers can access only cases they created or are members of
View and export all searches in the case
Add herself to the case as a member
questions.explain: Members of the eDiscovery Manager subgroup see only cases they created or were added to. eDiscovery Administrators can access all cases and add themselves as members, and only administrators can remove case members.

questions.case: Your E3 tenant does not have Defender for Office 365 Plan 2. A member of the eDiscovery Manager role group created a search that finds a phishing email in 600 mailboxes. When she runs New-ComplianceSearchAction -Purge, PowerShell reports that no parameter matches the name Purge.
questions.stem: What should you do so the purge can run?
options: Assign her the eDiscovery Administrator role
Assign her the Search And Purge role
Add her to the Organization Management role group in the Exchange admin center
Add her to the Reviewer role group
questions.explain: Purging requires the Search And Purge role (found in the Purview Organization Management role group). eDiscovery Administrator does not include it, Exchange Online Organization Management membership is not sufficient, and Reviewer only grants access to review sets.

questions.stem: You need to remove a phishing message from mailboxes using Security & Compliance PowerShell. Put the steps in order.
options: Confirm the item count with Get-ComplianceSearch
questions.explain: You connect to a search-only session, create and start the search, confirm the item count before deleting anything, and only then run New-ComplianceSearchAction -Purge. Status is then checked with Get-ComplianceSearchAction on the <search name>_Purge object.

questions.stem: Which statements about purging email with New-ComplianceSearchAction in a tenant without premium eDiscovery features are true? Select THREE.
options: A maximum of 10 items per mailbox is removed in one purge action
-PurgeType SoftDelete moves items to the Recoverable Items (Deletions) folder
It can also delete matching files from SharePoint and OneDrive
Items on litigation hold are permanently deleted
questions.explain: Each non-premium purge removes up to 10 items per mailbox, SoftDelete sends items to Recoverable Items (Deletions), and unindexed items are skipped. The action supports only Exchange Online mailboxes and public folders, and items on hold are preserved rather than permanently deleted.

questions.stem: You want to hunt for malicious Microsoft Graph API calls made by apps in your tenant. Which license is required to collect Microsoft Graph activity logs?
options: Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2
questions.explain: Microsoft Graph activity logs require a Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 tenant license plus an Azure subscription for the destination. Audit (Premium) and Defender for Cloud Apps are not the prerequisite, and Sentinel pricing tiers relate to ingestion, not to enabling the logs.

questions.case: Your SOC uses Microsoft Sentinel. You must be able to run KQL queries against Microsoft Graph activity logs and build analytics rules on them.
questions.stem: How should you configure collection?
options: Turn on Audit (Premium) and search the Graph operations in the Purview audit log
Create a diagnostic setting that sends Microsoft Graph activity logs to the Sentinel Log Analytics workspace
Create a diagnostic setting that archives Microsoft Graph activity logs to an Azure Storage account
Enable the Microsoft Graph Security API connector for alerts
questions.explain: Graph activity logs are streamed through diagnostic settings; sending them to a Log Analytics workspace creates the MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs table for KQL and Sentinel rules. Storage accounts suit long-term archive, not KQL. Purview audit does not hold these logs, and the Graph Security API connector ingests alerts, not request logs.

questions.stem: You want the apps, service principals and users with the most failed (401 or 403) Graph requests to /users over three days. Complete the KQL query.
questions.code:
MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs
| where TimeGenerated >= ago(3d)
| where ResponseStatusCode in (401, 403)
| where RequestUri contains "/users"
| ____ FailedRequests = count() by AppId, ServicePrincipalId, UserId
| sort by FailedRequests desc
questions.explain: summarize applies the count() aggregation grouped by AppId, ServicePrincipalId and UserId. project and extend do not accept 'by' grouping with aggregates, and distinct returns unique combinations without counts.

questions.stem: For each statement about Microsoft Graph activity logs, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

statements.s: Security Administrator is the least-privileged role that can configure the diagnostic setting for Microsoft Graph activity logs.
You can join Graph activity logs to sign-in logs by matching SignInActivityId to UniqueTokenIdentifier.
You can filter out unwanted Graph request types directly in the diagnostic setting to cut costs.

questions.explain: Security Administrator is the least-privileged supported role for setting this up. SignInActivityId joins to UniqueTokenIdentifier in the sign-in log tables. Diagnostic settings do not support filtering; to reduce cost, use a workspace transformation on the table.

questions.stem: You need to hunt for powershell.exe launched with an encoded command line on onboarded endpoints. Which advanced hunting table should you query?
questions.explain: DeviceProcessEvents records process creation with FileName and ProcessCommandLine. DeviceEvents holds security-control events (antivirus, exploit protection), DeviceImageLoadEvents holds DLL loads, and DeviceRegistryEvents holds registry changes.

questions.stem: A phishing campaign delivered a malicious link. You must identify which users actually clicked the Safe Links-wrapped URL. Which table should you query?
questions.explain: UrlClickEvents records Safe Links clicks from email, Teams and Office apps. EmailUrlInfo only lists URLs contained in messages, EmailPostDeliveryEvents covers post-delivery actions such as ZAP, and CloudAppEvents covers SaaS activity.

questions.stem: You need a query that lists each Defender XDR alert with its title and severity together with the files, IP addresses and users attached to it. Which TWO tables should you join? Select TWO.
questions.explain: AlertInfo has one row per alert (title, severity, category) and AlertEvidence lists the entities tied to each alert; they join on AlertId. BehaviorInfo holds behaviors, not alerts, and IdentityInfo/DeviceInfo are entity inventories.

questions.stem: Complete the query to find values written to Run keys, a common persistence technique.
questions.code:
____
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == 'RegistryValueSet'
| where RegistryKey contains @'Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName
questions.explain: DeviceRegistryEvents holds registry creation and modification with RegistryKey, RegistryValueName and the RegistryValueSet action type. The other Device tables don't carry these registry columns.

questions.stem: For each statement about advanced hunting tables, select Yes if true.

statements.s: EntraIdSignInEvents contains both interactive and non-interactive Microsoft Entra sign-ins.
IdentityDirectoryEvents records events from on-premises Active Directory domain controllers.
EmailAttachmentInfo records URLs sent in Microsoft Teams messages.

questions.explain: EntraIdSignInEvents (replacing AADSignInEventsBeta) covers interactive and non-interactive sign-ins, and IdentityDirectoryEvents comes from Defender for Identity on domain controllers. Teams URLs are in MessageUrlInfo; EmailAttachmentInfo describes email attachments.

questions.case: Contoso runs Microsoft Defender for Identity sensors on all domain controllers. After a workstation compromise, the SOC suspects the attacker enumerated members of Domain Admins and other privileged groups over LDAP before moving laterally. The hunter wants to see which accounts and devices issued those directory lookups.
questions.stem: Which table should the hunter query first?
questions.explain: IdentityQueryEvents records queries for AD objects such as users and groups (LDAP, SAMR, DNS), which is reconnaissance. IdentityLogonEvents covers authentications, IdentityDirectoryEvents covers DC-side changes and system events, and DeviceLogonEvents covers sign-ins on endpoints.

questions.stem: Complete the query to list phishing messages that were delivered to mailboxes in the last 7 days.
questions.code:
____
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ThreatTypes has 'Phish' and DeliveryAction == 'Delivered'
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject
questions.explain: EmailEvents holds delivery and blocking events with ThreatTypes, DeliveryAction, sender, recipient and Subject. EmailPostDeliveryEvents covers actions after delivery, EmailUrlInfo lists URLs, and CloudAppEvents covers cloud app activity.

questions.stem: Complete the query so it only returns events from the last 7 days.
questions.code:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ____(7d)
| where FileName =~ 'powershell.exe' and ProcessCommandLine has '-enc'
questions.explain: ago(7d) returns the current UTC time minus 7 days. now(7d) would be 7 days in the future, bin() needs a value and bucket size, and datetime() expects a date literal, not a timespan.

questions.stem: You want failed device logons counted per account for each hour to spot password-spray bursts. Complete the query.
questions.code:
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType == 'LogonFailed'
| summarize Failures = count() by AccountName, ____(Timestamp, 1h)
questions.explain: bin(Timestamp, 1h) rounds each timestamp down to the hour so summarize groups counts per hour. ago() takes one timespan, make_set is an aggregation not a grouping key, and todatetime() takes one argument.

questions.stem: A hunting query that uses `where ProcessCommandLine contains 'mimikatz'` over 30 days is slow and close to the CPU quota. You want to match the whole term faster. What should you change?
options: Add take 100 before the where clause
questions.explain: has matches whole terms using the term index, so it is much faster than substring contains. matches regex is slower still, =~ requires the entire value to equal the string, and take before where samples random rows and misses results.

questions.stem: Complete the query to return the 10 devices with the most successful outbound RDP connections.
questions.code:
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 3389 and ActionType == 'ConnectionSuccess'
| summarize Connections = count() by DeviceName
| ____ 10 by Connections desc
questions.explain: top N by Column desc returns the N highest rows by that column. take and limit return arbitrary N rows and don't accept a by clause, and sort by orders rows but doesn't take a count.

questions.stem: For each statement about KQL operators, select Yes if true.

statements.s: The =~ operator performs a case-insensitive equality comparison.
project adds calculated columns while keeping every existing column in the output.
summarize count() without a by clause returns a single row.

questions.explain: =~ is case-insensitive equality. Adding columns while keeping the rest is extend; project keeps only the columns you list. summarize without by aggregates the whole input into one row.

questions.stem: You want to find cmd.exe child processes launched between midnight and 06:00 UTC. Complete the query.
questions.code:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| ____ Hour = hourofday(Timestamp)
| where Hour < 6 and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ 'cmd.exe'
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, Hour
questions.explain: extend creates the calculated Hour column while keeping DeviceName, AccountName and the other columns used later. where filters rather than defines columns, order sorts, and evaluate invokes plugins.

questions.stem: Which KQL operator keeps only the columns you name (optionally renaming them) and drops all the others?
questions.explain: project outputs only the listed columns. extend adds columns and keeps the rest, distinct returns unique combinations of the named columns (deduplicating rows), and summarize aggregates rows into groups.

questions.stem: You want to find email attachments that were later written to disk on an endpoint. Complete the join condition.
questions.code:
EmailAttachmentInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d) and ActionType == 'FileCreated'
) on ____
| project Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, DeviceName, FileName, SHA256
questions.explain: Both tables carry the file hash in SHA256, so joining on it links the attachment to the file event. NetworkMessageId exists only on the email side, DeviceId only on the endpoint side, and ReportId identifies events within a table and doesn't link them.

questions.stem: DeviceInfo contains many snapshot rows per device. You need the most recent row, with all columns, for each DeviceId. Which aggregation should you use in summarize ... by DeviceId?
questions.explain: arg_max(Timestamp, *) returns the full row with the latest Timestamp per group. max(Timestamp) returns only the time, take_any returns an arbitrary row, and arg_min returns the earliest row.

questions.stem: For each device and account, you need a list of the distinct command lines executed in the last day. Complete the query.
questions.code:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| summarize Commands = ____(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, AccountName
questions.explain: make_set returns a dynamic array of distinct values. dcount returns only the number of distinct values, arg_min needs a column to minimise and returns a row, and countif needs a Boolean predicate.

questions.stem: You want to enrich executed binaries with global prevalence data and keep only rare files. Complete the query.
questions.code:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| distinct SHA1
| ____ FileProfile(SHA1, 1000)
| where GlobalPrevalence < 50
questions.explain: FileProfile() is an advanced hunting function applied to a tabular input with invoke; it adds columns such as GlobalPrevalence. evaluate calls plugins, lookup joins to a table, and extend can't call a tabular function.

questions.stem: You build a list of devices that ran a new remote management tool and want only those devices that do NOT appear in an approved-admin-devices list. Which join kind should you use with the device list on the left?
questions.explain: leftanti returns left rows that have no match on the right, i.e. devices not in the approved list. leftsemi returns only matching left rows, leftouter returns all left rows with or without matches, and innerunique is the default matching join.

questions.stem: For each statement about KQL, select Yes if true.

statements.s: If you don't specify kind, a KQL join uses the innerunique flavor.
Each let statement must end with a semicolon.
union fails unless all input tables have identical schemas.

questions.explain: innerunique is the default join kind, and let statements are terminated by a semicolon. union accepts tables with different schemas; columns missing from a table are simply empty for its rows.

questions.stem: How far back can an advanced hunting query look in native Microsoft Defender XDR data?
questions.explain: Advanced hunting keeps 30 days of native Defender XDR data. Longer history requires sending the data to a Microsoft Sentinel workspace with longer analytics-tier retention or streaming it elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements describe per-query limits in Defender XDR advanced hunting? Select TWO.
options: A query returns at most 100,000 rows.
A query returns at most 10,000 rows.
A query times out after 10 minutes.
A query can run for up to 1 hour.
Result sets are capped at 1 GB.
questions.explain: Advanced hunting returns up to 100,000 rows and 64 MB per query, and queries time out after 10 minutes. 10,000 rows, a 1-hour runtime and 1 GB aren't the documented per-query limits.

questions.stem: A new analyst who doesn't know KQL needs to build a hunting query by selecting fields and conditions. Which advanced hunting option should they use?
questions.explain: Guided mode is the query builder for users not yet familiar with KQL. Advanced mode expects hand-written KQL, custom detection rules schedule existing queries, and threat analytics is a reporting experience.

questions.stem: For each statement about advanced hunting in the Defender portal, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Advanced hunting evaluates all data in UTC.
Data stored only in the Microsoft Sentinel data lake tier can be queried directly in advanced hunting.
Tables from an onboarded Microsoft Sentinel workspace can be queried alongside Defender XDR tables.

questions.explain: Advanced hunting uses UTC and converts results to your display timezone. Onboarded Sentinel workspace tables appear in the schema, but lake-only data must be queried through data lake exploration, not advanced hunting.

questions.case: Fabrikam's incident responders regularly need to hunt DeviceProcessEvents and EmailEvents data that is four to six months old. They currently use only Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting and find that older data is missing. Fabrikam already licenses Microsoft Sentinel.
questions.stem: What should you do so the responders can hunt this older data from the Defender portal?
options: Turn on guided mode for the responders
Increase the retention period in Settings > Endpoints > Advanced features
Enable aggregated reporting for Defender for Endpoint
Ingest the Defender XDR tables into a Sentinel workspace onboarded to the Defender portal and set analytics-tier retention
questions.explain: Native advanced hunting keeps 30 days. Ingesting Defender XDR data into an onboarded Sentinel workspace makes it queryable for as long as the analytics-tier retention allows. Guided mode and aggregated reporting don't extend retention, and there is no Endpoints setting to do so.

questions.stem: You are converting an aggregated hunting query into a custom detection rule. The rule needs the Timestamp and ReportId of the most recent matching event per device. Complete the query.
questions.code:
DeviceEvents
| where ActionType == 'AntivirusDetection'
| summarize (Timestamp, ReportId) = ____(Timestamp, ReportId), count() by DeviceId
| where count_ > 5
questions.explain: arg_max(Timestamp, ReportId) returns the latest Timestamp and its ReportId, giving the rule the columns it needs. arg_min returns the earliest event, make_set returns an array, and dcount returns a number.

questions.stem: A custom detection rule on Defender XDR data is set to run every hour. What lookback period does each run cover?
questions.explain: Hourly rules look back 4 hours. Rules every 3 hours look back 12 hours, every 12 hours look back 48 hours, and every 24 hours look back 30 days.

questions.stem: You want a custom detection rule to use the Continuous (NRT) frequency. Which TWO requirements must the query meet? Select TWO.
options: It references only a single table.
It contains no join or union operators.
It queries only Microsoft Sentinel tables.
questions.explain: NRT rules must reference one table and avoid joins, unions and externaldata. They don't need summarize or a SHA256 column, and supported tables include Defender tables such as DeviceProcessEvents, not only Sentinel tables.

questions.case: A hunter wrote a query against DeviceNetworkEvents that finds devices beaconing to a known command-and-control domain. The SOC manager wants a custom detection rule that automatically isolates each affected device. The query currently projects Timestamp, ReportId, DeviceName and RemoteUrl.
questions.stem: Which column must you add to the query output so the Isolate device action can run?
questions.explain: Device response actions such as isolation use DeviceId, which Defender for Endpoint tables also need for correct scoping. AccountSid supports user actions, SHA1 columns support file actions, and NetworkMessageId supports email actions.

questions.stem: You need to turn an advanced hunting query into a custom detection rule. Put the steps in order.
options: Run the query and confirm it returns Timestamp, ReportId and entity columns
Enter alert details such as name, frequency, severity and MITRE techniques
Select response actions and scope, then review and create
questions.explain: You first validate the query output, then open the wizard from the editor, fill in alert details, map impacted entities, and finally choose actions and scope before creating the rule.

questions.stem: Which threat analytics report type describes a Microsoft-tracked threat actor's motivations, targets and tactics, techniques and procedures?
questions.explain: Actor reports profile a tracked threat actor. Activity reports cover a specific campaign, Tool reports cover malware or tools, and Technique reports cover a single attack technique.

questions.stem: You are reading a threat analytics report and want KQL vetted by Microsoft analysts that you can run in advanced hunting. Where do you find it?
options: The Detections/Hunting queries section of the Analyst report
questions.explain: The Analyst report includes a Detections/Hunting queries section with queries you can open in advanced hunting or turn into custom detections. The other tabs list assets, mitigations and incidents.

questions.stem: Which THREE sections appear on the threat analytics dashboard? Select THREE.
questions.explain: The dashboard shows Latest threats, High-impact threats (most alerts) and Highest exposure threats (vulnerability severity and exploitable devices). Top targeted users and Secure Score threats aren't dashboard sections.

questions.stem: For each statement about threat analytics, select Yes if true.

statements.s: A Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 1 licence on its own grants access to threat analytics.
Highest exposure threats are ranked using vulnerability severity and the number of devices that could be exploited.
Impacted assets counts distinct assets that have at least one active alert related to the threat.

questions.explain: Threat analytics needs a supported Defender product licence and Defender for Endpoint P1 alone doesn't qualify. Exposure ranking uses vulnerability severity and exploitable device count, and Impacted assets counts assets with active alerts.

questions.case: Microsoft publishes a threat analytics report about a ransomware group exploiting a VPN vulnerability. The CISO asks two things: has the group been active in our tenant, and which of our devices are still vulnerable? The analyst has Security data basics (read), Vulnerability management (read) and Exposure Management (read).
questions.stem: Which report tab answers the second question?
questions.explain: Endpoints exposure shows devices vulnerable to the threat (requires Vulnerability management read). Related incidents answers the first question, Overview shows alert trends, and the Analyst report is Microsoft's write-up rather than tenant-specific device data.

questions.stem: Where do you create a new hunting graph in the Microsoft Defender portal?
options: Advanced hunting, then Create new > Hunting graph
Incidents, select a node, then View blast radius
Microsoft Sentinel > Threat management > Hunting > Hunts
questions.explain: The hunting graph opens from advanced hunting through the graph icon or Create new > Hunting graph. View blast radius is on the incident graph, the attack surface map belongs to Exposure Management, and Hunts track Sentinel hunting hypotheses.

questions.stem: You need to check whether a compromised workstation has any route to a specific storage account. Which hunting graph predefined scenario fits best?
options: Choke points to SQL data stores
questions.explain: Paths between two entities tests whether a path exists between a chosen start and target. Entity relationship map shows only direct connections of one entity, choke points looks at SQL stores generally, and the critical identities scenario focuses on privileged users.

questions.stem: An analyst can run advanced hunting queries but sees no hunting graph option. Which TWO prerequisites should you check? Select TWO.
options: The tenant is onboarded to the Microsoft Sentinel data lake.
The analyst has at least read access in Microsoft Security Exposure Management.
The analyst has Security Copilot Contributor.
Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management is enabled.
Defender for Endpoint Plan 1 is assigned.
questions.explain: The hunting graph needs an onboarded Sentinel data lake and at least read-only Exposure Management access, plus advanced hunting permissions. Security Copilot, Insider Risk Management and Defender for Endpoint P1 aren't prerequisites.

questions.stem: You need to review the potential impact of a compromised user during an incident. Put the steps in order.
options: Open the incident from the Incidents page
Select the compromised user node on the incident graph
Review the top-rated paths, then open View full blast radius list
questions.explain: Blast radius starts on the incident graph: open the incident, select the node, choose View blast radius (which loads the eight top-rated paths), then expand to the full list for all targets.

questions.stem: For each statement about blast radius analysis, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Blast radius shows the exact path the attacker used after the compromise.
Blast radius results are scoped by the viewing user's permissions.
Viewing blast radius requires Exposure management (read) permission or higher.

questions.explain: Blast radius shows possible propagation paths, not confirmed attacker activity. Nodes and edges outside the user's RBAC scope are hidden, and Exposure management (read) or higher is required.

questions.case: Tailspin Toys onboarded the Sentinel data lake and the SOC uses blast radius during incidents. Analysts complain that blast radius rarely shows paths to the payroll database servers or the finance key vault, even though many admins can reach them. Nobody has configured anything in Microsoft Security Exposure Management since onboarding.
questions.stem: What should you do first to improve the blast radius results?
options: Review and classify the critical assets in Microsoft Security Exposure Management
Increase the analytics-tier retention of the Sentinel workspace
Create a custom detection rule for the payroll servers
questions.explain: Blast radius calculates paths to critical targets; if critical assets aren't classified in Exposure Management, the graph under-represents risk. UEBA, retention and custom detections don't define path targets.

questions.stem: You want to find identities that have an edge to a virtual machine in the exposure graph. Complete the query.
questions.code:
ExposureGraphEdges
| ____ SourceNodeId --> TargetNodeId with ExposureGraphNodes on NodeId
| graph-match (Identity)-[e]->(Vm)
    where set_has_element(Identity.Categories, 'identity') and set_has_element(Vm.Categories, 'virtual_machine')
    project IdentityName = Identity.NodeName, VmName = Vm.NodeName, Edge = e.EdgeLabel
questions.explain: make-graph builds a graph from the edges table, using ExposureGraphNodes for node properties, which graph-match then searches. make-series builds time series, graph-to-table converts a graph back to tables, and mv-expand expands arrays.

questions.stem: You built a custom graph in Microsoft Sentinel from data lake tables and materialised it with a graph job. Which language do you use to query it on the Graphs page in the Defender portal?
questions.explain: Sentinel custom graphs are queried with Graph Query Language (GQL). KQL graph operators work on tables such as ExposureGraphEdges, Gremlin is used by Azure Cosmos DB graphs, and T-SQL is for SQL databases.

questions.stem: Which THREE experiences are powered by Microsoft Sentinel graph? Select THREE.
options: Blast radius on the Defender incident graph
Attack paths in Microsoft Security Exposure Management
questions.explain: Sentinel graph powers blast radius, the hunting graph and Exposure Management attack paths (as well as Purview data risk graphs). Secure Score is a posture score, and livestream has been retired from Sentinel.

questions.stem: In Microsoft Sentinel hunting, a query shows N/A in the Results column. What does this indicate?
options: The query has no active data source connected
The query was disabled by an administrator
questions.explain: N/A means the data source the query needs isn't connected or active; hovering the info icon shows which sources are required. Zero results show as 0, and N/A doesn't indicate a timeout or a disabled query.

questions.stem: You want to quickly see which hunting queries have changed the most in the last day compared with the day before. Which column should you sort by?
questions.explain: Results delta compares the last 24 hours with the previous 24 to 48 hours, highlighting spikes. Results is the absolute count, and Techniques and Data source describe the query rather than change over time.

questions.stem: You want to adjust the KQL of a built-in hunting query that was installed from a Content hub solution. What should you do?
options: Select Edit and change the Query field
Delete the solution and recreate the query
Clone the query and edit the clone
Export the query to a workbook and edit it there
questions.explain: Only queries from a custom content source can be edited; Content hub queries are cloned and the clone is modified. Deleting the solution or exporting to a workbook isn't the supported approach.

questions.stem: You need to create a custom hunting query in Microsoft Sentinel in the Defender portal. Put the steps in order.
options: Go to Microsoft Sentinel > Threat management > Hunting
Select the Queries tab and then New query
Enter the name, description and KQL query
Configure entity mappings and MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques
questions.explain: Custom hunting queries are created from the Hunting page's Queries tab with New query; you fill in the query details, map entities and MITRE ATT&CK, then select Create.

questions.stem: For each statement about Microsoft Sentinel hunting queries, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Installing a Content hub solution can add hunting queries to the Queries tab.
Favourited hunting queries run automatically when the Hunting page is opened.
Hunting queries are written in a language different from the one used by analytics rules.

questions.explain: Solutions install out-of-the-box hunting queries, and favourites run automatically when the page opens. Hunting queries and analytics rules both use KQL.

questions.case: During weekly hunting, an analyst at Northwind finds that a custom hunting query for suspicious service creation reliably finds real attacks with few false positives. The SOC wants this logic to raise incidents automatically every hour, with the same entity mappings.
questions.stem: What should the analyst do?
options: Add the query to a hunt and set its status to Active
Bookmark the results and create an incident
Start a livestream session for the query
Right-click the query and select Create analytics rule
questions.explain: Create analytics rule turns the hunting query into a scheduled rule that generates alerts and incidents. A hunt only tracks investigation, a bookmark handles one set of results, and livestream is no longer available in Sentinel.

questions.stem: You are writing a Sentinel hunting query for accounts with many failed Microsoft Entra sign-ins. Complete the time filter for the Sentinel table.
questions.code:
SigninLogs
| where ____ > ago(1d)
| where ResultType != '0'
| summarize Failures = count() by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| where Failures > 20
questions.explain: Sentinel (Log Analytics) tables such as SigninLogs use TimeGenerated. Timestamp is the Defender XDR advanced hunting column, EventTime isn't a SigninLogs column, and _BinStartTime appears only in summary rule output.

questions.stem: In which Log Analytics table are Microsoft Sentinel hunting bookmarks stored?
questions.explain: Bookmarks are written to the HuntingBookmark table. SecurityIncident and SecurityAlert hold incidents and alerts, and Watchlist holds watchlist items.

questions.stem: Which THREE items does a Microsoft Sentinel bookmark preserve or let you add? Select THREE.
options: The query that produced the rows
Entity mappings and MITRE ATT&CK tactics
An automatic isolation action for mapped hosts
The time range of the results
questions.explain: A bookmark keeps the rows, the originating query and the time range, and you can add entities, MITRE mappings, tags and notes. Bookmarks don't isolate hosts or schedule reruns; use analytics rules, KQL jobs or playbooks for that.

questions.stem: For each statement about hunts in Microsoft Sentinel, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Queries added to a hunt are cloned, so editing them doesn't change the original workspace queries.
Each hunt has Queries, Bookmarks and Entities tabs.
Bookmarks can be created from Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting results.

questions.explain: Hunts use independent clones and have Queries, Bookmarks and Entities tabs. Bookmarks are a Sentinel hunting feature and aren't available in Defender advanced hunting; alternatives there include saved queries and incident tags.

questions.case: A SOC lead used to keep a Microsoft Sentinel livestream open to watch for a newly disclosed exploit pattern and wants equivalent continuous monitoring, with results that persist and notifications sent to a Teams channel. Livestream is no longer available in the tenant.
questions.stem: Which approach best replaces the livestream?
options: Bookmark the current results and add them to a hunt
Pin the hunting query as a favourite
Create a near-real-time analytics rule from the query and attach a playbook that posts to Teams
Create a workbook tile that runs the query
questions.explain: Microsoft recommends analytics rules (or KQL jobs) with playbooks as livestream replacements, giving persistent results and messaging integration. Bookmarks and favourites don't monitor continuously, and a workbook tile only runs when someone views it.

questions.stem: You are running a hypothesis-driven hunt in Microsoft Sentinel. Put the steps in order.
options: Create a new hunt and record the hypothesis
Add and run relevant hunting queries in the hunt
Create an incident from the bookmarks
Set the hypothesis state and hunt status when finished
questions.explain: A hunt starts with a hypothesis, then runs queries, captures evidence as bookmarks, escalates real findings to incidents, and closes by recording whether the hypothesis was validated.

questions.stem: A KQL job writes its results to a new table in the analytics tier named IOCMatches. What is the full name of the created table?
questions.explain: New analytics-tier tables from KQL jobs get the _KQL_CL suffix; _KQL is used for data lake tier tables. _SPRK_CL is for notebook output and plain _CL for summary rules and custom logs.

questions.stem: Which TWO functions are NOT supported in Microsoft Sentinel data lake KQL jobs? Select TWO.
questions.explain: KQL jobs don't support externaldata(), ingestion_time(), adx(), arg() or user-defined functions. ago(), bin() and summarize are standard KQL and are supported.

questions.stem: A scheduled KQL job runs every 15 minutes. Because lake data can take up to 15 minutes to become queryable, you offset the window. Complete the query.
questions.explain: now() minus the delay sets the window end 15 minutes in the past. ago(15m) would double the delay, ingestion_time() isn't supported in KQL jobs and isn't a scalar for the current time, and startofday() would fix the window to midnight.

questions.stem: For each statement about KQL jobs, select Yes if true.

statements.s: When more than five KQL jobs try to run at the same time in a tenant, the extra runs are queued until a slot frees.
A KQL job can append results to an existing analytics-tier table only if the schema matches.
A scheduled KQL job's start time must be at least 30 minutes after it is created or edited.

questions.explain: The limit is 5 concurrent executions per tenant and excess requests are rejected, not queued. Appending requires a matching schema, and scheduled jobs must start at least 30 minutes after creation or editing.

questions.case: Litware keeps two years of firewall logs in the Microsoft Sentinel data lake tier only. Each morning the threat intelligence team publishes new indicators. The SOC wants every new indicator checked against the last 90 days of firewall logs, with matches written to a table that an analytics rule can alert on.
questions.stem: What should you create?
options: A summary rule on the firewall table
A custom detection rule in advanced hunting
A scheduled Microsoft Sentinel hunting query marked as a favourite
A daily scheduled KQL job that writes matches to an analytics-tier table
questions.explain: KQL jobs query long history in the data lake and promote results to analytics-tier tables for analytics rules. Summary rules only process recent bins, custom detections can't read lake-only data, and favouriting a hunting query doesn't schedule it or persist results.

questions.stem: Which table plan does a Microsoft Sentinel summary rule's destination table use?
questions.explain: Summary rule results land in a custom _CL table on the Analytics plan, so they are fast to query and alert on. The source data, by contrast, can be on Basic or Auxiliary plans.

questions.stem: You are writing the KQL for a new summary rule with an hourly bin size. A colleague adds `| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)` to the query. What should you do?
options: Keep it, because summary rules process the whole table without it
Remove it, because the bin size already defines the time range
Change it to ago(24h) to cover the maximum delay
questions.explain: Summary rule queries shouldn't contain a time filter; each run operates over the window defined by the bin size. Adding ago() filters or ingestion_time() conflicts with the bin logic.

questions.stem: A summary rule wrote aggregated connection counts to NetSummary_CL. Complete the hunting query so it filters by the start of each aggregation bin.
questions.code:
NetSummary_CL
| where ____ > ago(7d)
| where DestinationIP == '203.0.113.50'
| project _BinStartTime, SourceIP, DestinationIP, Connections
questions.explain: Summary rule output includes _BinStartTime, the start of the aggregation interval, along with _BinSize and _RuleName. Timestamp is a Defender XDR column, and _TimeReceived and ingestion_time() reflect pipeline timing rather than the bin.

questions.stem: For each statement about summary rules, select Yes if true.

statements.s: A summary rule can use a bin size of 24 hours (1440 minutes).
A summary rule can reprocess the previous 90 days of data when it is first created.
Creating summary rules requires the Microsoft Sentinel Contributor role.

questions.explain: Bin sizes range from 20 to 1440 minutes. Summary rules don't allow historical time ranges; they process recent data only (a KQL job suits backfill). Microsoft Sentinel Contributor is required.

questions.case: Adatum ingests about 4 TB per day of proxy logs and stores them on the Auxiliary plan to save cost. Analysts need fast hourly per-user request counts for hunting, and an analytics rule must alert when a user's hourly count exceeds a threshold. Queries on the raw table are slow and incur scan charges.
questions.stem: What should you implement?
options: A summary rule with a 60-minute bin size writing to a custom _CL table
A hunting query marked as a favourite on the raw table
A KQL job that runs once against the last 12 years of data
An NRT custom detection rule on the raw table
questions.explain: A summary rule aggregates the Auxiliary data each hour into a small Analytics table that hunts and analytics rules query quickly and cheaply. Favourites still scan the raw table, a one-time KQL job doesn't keep up hourly, and an NRT detection gives alerts but no aggregated table for hunting.

questions.stem: In a Microsoft Sentinel data lake notebook, complete the code that loads a table into a Spark DataFrame.
questions.code:
from sentinel_lake.providers import MicrosoftSentinelProvider
data_provider = MicrosoftSentinelProvider(spark)
df = data_provider.____('SigninLogs', 'ContosoWorkspace')
questions.explain: read_table(table_name, database_name) returns a Spark DataFrame. load_table isn't a provider method, query_lake is a Sentinel MCP tool, and list_tables returns table names rather than data.

questions.stem: A notebook must append scored results to a new analytics-tier table. Which table name is valid for save_as_table?
questions.explain: Notebook writes to the analytics tier use the _SPRK_CL suffix; _SPRK is for the data lake tier. _KQL_CL is for KQL jobs, and plain _CL is for summary rules and custom logs.

questions.stem: You are planning notebook-based hunting on the Microsoft Sentinel data lake. Which TWO statements are true? Select TWO.
options: The overwrite write mode is supported only for data lake tier tables.
You can pip install any Python package into the Spark session.
Notebooks run in Visual Studio Code with the Microsoft Sentinel extension on a Small, Medium or Large pool.
Notebook jobs have no timeout and unlimited concurrency.
questions.explain: overwrite works only in the lake tier (analytics supports append), and notebooks run in VS Code with the Sentinel extension on a chosen pool size. Custom pip installs aren't supported, notebook jobs time out after 8 hours with 3 running at once, and delete_table removes lake _SPRK tables only.

questions.stem: You need to connect Visual Studio Code to the Microsoft Sentinel MCP server data exploration tools. Put the steps in order.
options: Run MCP: Add Server from the command palette
Select HTTP as the transport type
Enter the data exploration collection URL and a server ID
Sign in with an account that has at least Security Reader
Open Chat in Agent mode and confirm the tools under Configure Tools
questions.explain: You add the server from the command palette, choose HTTP, paste the collection URL and name it, authenticate with at least Security Reader, then verify the tools in agent mode chat.

questions.stem: An AI agent connected to the Microsoft Sentinel MCP server needs a workspace ID before running other tools. Which tool should it call first?
questions.explain: list_sentinel_workspaces returns the workspace name and ID pairs you can access and is meant to run first. search_tables finds relevant tables, query_lake runs KQL, and get_entity_analysis retrieves an entity analysis result.

questions.case: An analyst connected GitHub Copilot in VS Code to the Sentinel MCP data exploration collection with a Security Reader account. search_tables and query_lake work, but every call to analyze_user_entity fails with a permissions error.
questions.stem: Which additional role should the analyst be assigned?
questions.explain: Entity analyzer tools consume Security Compute Units, so they require the Security Copilot Contributor role. Sentinel Contributor and Log Analytics Contributor govern workspace content, and Security Administrator isn't the documented requirement for the analyzers.

questions.stem: Which Microsoft Sentinel MCP data exploration tool runs a KQL query against data in the Sentinel data lake?
questions.explain: query_lake runs a single KQL query against a data lake workspace and returns the results. search_tables finds tables and schemas, find_nodes searches graph nodes, and analyze_url_entity runs an AI analysis of a URL.
